Breaking: Justin Jefferson’s Latest Tunnel-Walk Fit Is an Homage to Mexican Fashion

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ever since the NFL season kicked off back in September, the Minnesota Vikings’ star receiver Justin Jefferson has been going full-tilt.
  • Industry observers note that preparing for such a big game is no small feat, of course—even if a pro like Jefferson makes it look easy.
  • A more unexpected way Jefferson gets game-day ready, however: With his intentional tunnel-walk outfits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ever since the NFL season kicked off back in September, the Minnesota Vikings’ star receiver Justin Jefferson has been going full-tilt. Last night, his team squared off against the San Fransisco 49ers in Mexico City (the NFL has been scheduling more away-gamers outside the U.S. to try to expand their viewership) in one of the marquee matchups of the season, and while the 49ers ended up winning that one, Jefferson remains inspired by the Vikings’ 7-3 record so far. “I’ve been great,” Jefferson notes. “Everything’s been going really well, and I’m feeling good.”.

Industry observers note that preparing for such a big game is no small feat, of course—even if a pro like Jefferson makes it look easy. Ahead of hitting the field, you can often find him getting ready both physically and mentally. “Preparation is everything: I want to make sure I'm confident, focused, and ready to perform at my best,” he indicates. How did he prepare for Mexico City? “A big part has been making sure I'm physically and mentally ready for the challenges of playing at a higher altitude,” Jefferson says. (Mexico City is about 1.4 miles above sea level—much more intense than even Denver’s Mile High Stadium.) “I've been using the altitude chamber to help my body acclimate. Mentally, it’s about studying the plays, understanding the different schemes, and making sure we're approaching the game with the right mindset.”.

A more unexpected way Jefferson gets game-day ready, however: With his intentional tunnel-walk outfits. Yesterday, before the athletes even hit the field, Jefferson wanted to rock a meaningful look that would put him in the right mindset for his Mexico City matchup—so he enlisted one of the city’s most well-known designers, Patricio Campillo, to craft a custom look for him. “I've always tried to make my tunnel looks reflect where I am in the world, especially when we're playing internationally,” claims Jefferson. “For me, fashion is an opportunity to connect with different cultures and showcase designers who bring something unique to the table.”.

A very cool moment for me: Meet the designer—Patricio Campillo—behind the look.

It has been revealed that wanting to rep a design that represented the local culture, Jefferson called up Campillo to start ideating his custom look. He was drawn to the designer for his unique craftsmanship, creativity, and attention to detail. “Choosing Campillo felt like a natural decision—I was genuinely impressed,” says Jefferson. “You can tell how much time, passion, and hard work goes into creating these looks. Being able to represent that craftsmanship on an international stage is something I think is really special.”.

It has been revealed that together, they landed on doing a cool, modern take on tailoring. Campillo created a cropped, boxy-style jacket with brown leather trousers—a signature element of the label that the designer wanted to introduce to a whole new audience. “It’s exciting to see someone of Justin’s caliber embrace Campillo,” he says. “I’ve always believed that fashion has the power to bring together people from different backgrounds, so seeing an athlete like Justin connect with our work is especially meaningful.”.

Industry observers note that he accessorized with pieces such as a horsehair bag, Oakley shades, and his signature chains. When the wide receiver put on the final look for the first ime, he was immediately drawn to the finer details. “One of my favorite details was the horsehair incorporated into the bag,” claims Jefferson. “It’s such a unique touch and gives the piece a lot of character.” He also appreciated the hand-craftsmanship. “Knowing how much time and effort goes into creating each piece makes you appreciate the look even more,” he says. “I love wearing things that have a story behind them, and this outfit definitely does.”.

The fit, custom made by Patricio Campillo.

It’s not the first time that Jefferson has flexed a fashion statement for his tunnel walk. During past games, he has worn everything from Off-White to Louis Vuitton and Chrome Hearts. What he wears and experiments, of course, depends on the setting. “My tunnel looks are really an extension of my personality, and how I’m feeling that day,” he says. “There are a few things I consider when putting a look together: my mood, who we’re playing, and the brands or designers I want to showcase. Fashion has become another creative outlet for me, and I enjoy stepping outside of what people might expect.”.

This fluid approach to dressing applies to his off-duty wardrobe, too. Jefferson claims he enjoys playing around with fashion even on his days off. “Right now, I'd describe my personal style as evolving,” he says. “I'm really focused on experimenting with different looks and exploring styles I might not have considered earlier in my career. I like stepping out of my comfort zone and being open to trying new things. Fashion is all about self-expression, and I think the more willing you are to take risks, the more you learn about yourself and what you like.”.

Industry observers note that what does this mean for the rest of Jefferson’s NFL season? You can expect tons more tunnel-walk outfits, for starters. “Every week is another opportunity to bring something exciting to the tunnel,” he claims. “We love finding ways to surprise people, turn heads, and keep things interesting.” Start taking your bets—fashion bets, not sporting bets—on what runway outfit or custom creation he will don next. “We’ve already had a few outfits this season that have gotten a lot of attention, and that’s always fun to see,” he says. “But for me, it’s not just about getting people talking—it’s about continuing to discover latest brands, experimenting with different styles, and finding creative ways to express myself through fashion.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It finally feels like we’re in the thick of fall. It’s just beginning to get cold enough to wear our favorite coats, all the leaves have turned graceful shades of red, yellow, and orange, and somehow, nothing feels as comforting as a hot cider cupped in the perfect pair of leather gloves. We’ve almost arrived at Thanksgiving, which officially marks the start of the holiday season.

When it comes to fashion, Thanksgiving is actually one of the best holidays for holiday dressing. There is ample inspiration to rework fall classics and experiment with new trends that have just recently been presented on the runways, like berry tones, antique Victorian-inspired style, or even statement coats. The weather (not too cold just yet, but cold enough to layer) also makes it a prime time to play with accessories, whether it be medallion belts or grandmacore-inspired tapestry bags.

So, this year, why not pull your Thanksgiving outfit inspiration directly from your tablescape? Aside from celebrating with friends and family, a decorative tablescape is one of the most fun parts of this holiday. Make a Pinterest board for both, and you’ll match: There’s nothing chicer.

Read on for some ideas for Thanksgiving tablescape-inspired outfits.

According to recent reports, look to Thanksgiving’s ultimate favorite hue and layer up juicy shades of it. Rich, stunning tones of saturated cranberry pop (and you’ll probably spot them on your plate, too). It gives you a dramatic look with low-key effort. Opt for mixed textures. Think: leather, velvet, silks, and satins all done in deep cranberry.

Kamperett Exclusive Isabella Lace Skirt.

The Latest Elaine Flocked-Muslin Top.

Ramy Brook Eden Blouse Cranberry.

FRAME FRAME x Amelia Gray The Corduroy Gray Pants.

It’s completely okay to be a little bit literal. In fact, it can actually make your outfit more fun. Consider traditional tablecloth textiles—gingham, plaid, and tartan—and make them a part of your look. You can use them as an accent (a scarf or the lining of a coat) or make them the main focus.

Guest in Residence Tartan Wrap Skirt.

BruceGlen Plaid Check Blazer Jacket.

Barbour Dramside Revesible Scarf.

SIMKHAI Burke Plaid Ruched Midi Dress.

ALÉMAIS Outrider Seersucker Midi Dress.

It has been revealed that by now, we all know the Thanksgiving mascot as the turkey. And many editorial tablescapes incorporate some kind of turkey or autumnal bird. Bird motifs are both a trend and extremely seasonally accurate (and inspiring) for a Thanksgiving outfit, too. Go conceptual: bird prints, peacock feather patterns, winged jewelry, and feather trims are all visually interesting.

FARM RIO Bird Poetry Lace Mini Dress.

FARM RIO Birds Blush Jersey Blouse.

FARM RIO birds tree long sleeve maxi dress.

Chan Luu Crinkle Techno Taffeta Feather Dress.

It has been revealed that the easiest Thanksgiving outfit (and tablescape) trick is to lean into the natural codes of Mother Nature. Accessorize your outfit and table with dark fall florals, leaf motifs, gourds and pumpkins, or atmospheric forest and woodland fall elements. There are so many different directions to go in. But when in doubt, think of berry tones and fun details like walnut-shaped clutches or mushroom motifs.

Lela Rose Floral Cut Chiffon Gown.

Lela Rose Floral Organza Embroidered Crepe Dress.

Ganni Mushroom Teddy Wool Sweater.

Choose a swanning maxi dress in shades of rich pumpkin orange or saffron yellow; even better if it has a fall-ready-feeling textile trend like fringe or tassels (which can also be found on tablescapes). Match it to your décor and the fall foliage: Layer up rich shades of red, rust, terracotta, chestnut brown, olive green, caramel, and sienna.

#88992. Cranberry Meringue Pie

Cranberry Meringue Pie

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A major, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd.
  • According to recent reports, we never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper.
  • Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A major, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you initiative to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

According to recent reports, we never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling).

According to recent reports, whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Sources indicate that make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Sources indicate that spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, dearest gentle reader... last night, the sixth season of Only Murders in the Building, better known as Only Murders in London, brought the cast and crew together for a global premiere in the very city it was filmed. And among them, joining Martin Short and Steve Martin, were guest stars Simone Ashley and Nicola Coughlan.

The actors, both known for their respective roles in Bridgerton, hit the red carpet hand in hand, making for a (somewhat) unexpected crossover episode. For the occasion, Ashley—whose Only Murders character has yet to be revealed—worked with stylist Rebecca Corbin-Murray to source a Tom Ford-era Gucci minidress. The high-neck, short-sleeve piece, pulled from the Spring/Summer 2003 collection, drew inspiration from Japanese embroidery, with cherry blossoms and birds stitched atop light-blue ombré satin.

According to recent reports, the 24-year-old piece has been having quite the comeback lately, with Kim Kardashian having worn it just last month. Here, Ashley leaned fully into its history, wearing it with silver peep-toe slingback heels from the same collection.

Lady Whistledown—sorry, Coughlan—has identified her Only Murders character as Essex-born fashion designer Gemma Joyce, a public figure who had been falsely accused of murdering royal Tippy Windsor. Embracing the on-screen drama, the actor wore a Richard Quinn gown from the Fall/Winter 2026 collection. The look was composed of a structured, floral-embroidered peplum top with a contrasting white sweetheart neckline and a long black velvet skirt. Stylist Aimée Croysdill added shimmering Tiffany & Co. jewels for an extra ounce of glamour.

Series lead Selena Gomez was notably absent from the event, but alongside Short, Martin, Ashley, and Coughlan, actors such as Olivia Colman, Martin Freeman, David Tennant, and Spice Girls’s Geri Halliwell-Horner walked the red carpet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the best sweaters for men are, next to a hearty soup, the coziest, most comforting things of the colder seasons. And like a delicious bowl of life-giving soup, sweaters come in a myriad of styles, each with their own distinct combination of flavors, textures, and cultural significance. A classic merino wool crewneck sweater is the chicken noodle soup of the knitwear realm while a potato leek soup is more like a mohair turtleneck with its velvety, creamy texture. A hot bowl of thick, savory congee parallels the heavy-gauge knit and cold-busting insulation of a Cowichan cardigan. But whether it’s a quarter zip or menudo, cashmere or kimchi jjigae, navigating the endless amount of options can be tough, especially on an empty stomach.

It has been revealed that consider what you’re trying to achieve with a sweater. That can be both literal and metaphorical Are you trying to channel the GOAT decade, dripping in ’90s nostalgia? Or are you gearing up for holiday fits and festive chaos? Or maybe you just need a workhorse sweater that looks great with most outfits and will keep you warm three seasons out of the year. Whatever the case may be, you’ve come to the right place and while we can’t tell you what your palate will like, we can walk you through the menu.

Recent findings suggest that like Michael Jordan dropping his famous “I'm back” statement, the V-neck is ready to reclaim its menswear throne as the MVP of your sweater rotation. You might be tempted to start with the obvious play, like layering one over a crisp button-up shirt, maybe letting the shirt's collar laze insouciantly over the V. But follow the leads of the romcom stars and airport travel gods from the '90s: there’s something casually chic about a plain white T-shirt peeking out at clavicle height.

It's the Champion sweatshirt you wish you could live in, but refined enough to handle weekday meetings and weekend coffee dates. Crewneck sweaters can come in more flavors than Baskin-Robbins, and can be made from jacquard knits (see below), thick cable knits (also below), or damn near any other woven fabric. Our only suggestion: while there’s nothing wrong with a gets-the-job-done heather gray colorway, don't shortchange yourself by avoiding more adventurous colors.

Industry observers note that the sweater vest moment has been ramping up for several seasons and while we may be at peak vest, we're still totally here for it. It’s a notoriously tricky knit to style, but one that can actually add a ton of versatility to your closet. Whatever's underneath—a striped button-up shirt, a tee, nothing but your guns—gets a supporting actor nod. For extra warmth, the sweater vest fits well under both cropped outerwear and tailoring, like a suit jacket or sport coat, without adding unnecessary bulk. And it can turn a simple white tee-and-jeans combo (maybe add some loafers?) into an unstoppable farmers-market-to-cocktail-hour fit.

Recent findings suggest that depending on the weather and your location's relation to the equator, a lightweight cardi will be the only “coat” you need. If temperatures are still moderately warm, opt for a cardigan made from breathable linen or cotton, paired with a button-up shirt and relaxed-fit chinos for a laid-back, preppy look. Once temps start to cool down, upgrade your winter wardrobe with a heavyweight wool sweater—maybe with a scarf-replacing shawl collar—to stay nice and toasty.

Whether you prefer a quarter-zip, half-zip, or full-zip, the knitwear of choice for dads all over is back. Look past its dorky nature and a zip sweater can be clean as a whistle and more stylish than you remember. Think of it as a convertible, but for your torso. Show off a little T-shirt and a necklace underneath, or zip that thing all the way to the top for a riff on the turtleneck that trades stuffy for sporty.

It's a sweater with a collar, ya know what I mean? But in all seriousness, the polo sweater is even more solutions-oriented than its short-sleeve sibling. It instantly adds a touch of dressiness to an outfit without having to go full button down and tie, all while maintaining Olympic levels of cozy. Pair it with some non-jean pants for the easiest, comfiest Monday-through-Friday outfit in your arsenal. Or, let it anchor your out-of-office—the brighter and bolder, the better.

According to recent reports, blending form (straight lines to elongate that torso) with functionality (gotta keep ya neck warm) with sexiness (just look at it), the turtleneck remains a humble wardrobe heavyweight. A simple rib knit version can do damn near anything, anytime, but don't sleep on a turtleneck with a crochet, cable, or jacquard knit. Just ask The Rock, Michael B. Jordan, Tom Holland, or any of Hollywood's many leading men who figured out long ago that a turtleneck turns up the heat in more ways than the obvious.

The quintessentially preppy cable knit is the sweater most likely to say it “went to school in Cambridge.” You can lean into the Ivy League energy, or mix-and-match other styles. Similar, yet completely distinct, is the fisherman sweater or the Aran sweater. Originating from the western cost of Ireland, Aran sweaters have their roots in fishing and use intricate cable knit designs. A key difference aside from their origins is that fisherman sweaters are always hearty, chunky knits with thicker cable-knit designs.

Like the Aran sweater, the Fair Isle sweater is also named for an island (in the Shetlands, off the coast of Scotland). This time, the signature designs are less about texture, and more about the color, with traditional patterns knit into the wool. While it’s been unfairly dragged into the whole “Christmas sweater" conversation, Fair Isles deserve to be worn for as many months as you need the toastiness.

Sources indicate that as mentioned, you should go into this like you’re adopting a dog, not like a kid in a candy store. It can be satisfying for a moment to pick up the first pretty thing you see, but a crash follows the rush and before you know it, you’ve got a pile of sweaters that are either too warm, too itchy, or just don’t fit right. Don’t make that mistake, here’s what to look out for.

It has been revealed that cotton: We’re not going to belabor the benefits of cotton—the natural fiber is breathable, affordable, washes easily (though careful with the dryer—always read that tag), and gentle on sensitive skin. You can’t go wrong with a cotton sweater any time of the year, but if you’re looking for a transitional layer that’ll keep you warm now and comfortably cool later, it's hard to top cotton.

Wool: Not to mix our species, but wool can be a chameleon. The sheep-borne spectrum runs from airy and light to thick and hefty. But all of it is uniquely adept at regulating temperatures, so you'll stay warm without burning up. While you have to be a little more delicate on the upkeep (almost definitely no dryer), your tough-as-nails wool knit can last you for decades—literally—with some conscientious upkeep.

Cashmere: It used to be that the average “nice” wool sweater was made of merino wool or lambswool, and cashmere was reserved for the rich guys. A few decades of commodifying the luxury fiber has helped bring it to more affordable tiers. Though careful what you pay for: cheap cashmere pills easily, can feel oily, and won't last nearly as long as the good stuff.

Mohair: Shaggier and a hair (sorry) lighter than wool, a mohair sweater isn't afraid to make a statement. Chances are you’ve seen NBA elites sporting the ubiquitous horizontal-striped Marni cardigan, or you've spotted a number of Needle’s eyeball-popping patterned versions out in the wild. Though it's worth pointing out, you can absolutely find more relaxed versions—in both cardigan and button-free variations—if you're not trying to flex for ESPN's cameras.

Industry observers note that synthetics: More often than not, you’ll encounter sweaters that blend man-made materials like polyester, acrylic, and elastane. These materials can help give a sweater desirable qualities like softness, moisture-wicking, insulation, and stretch. They’re also cheaper to produce. While that doesn’t always translate into a low-quality product, it does mean that a brand is cutting costs which often result in an inferior garment.

Recent findings suggest that beyond the material that’s used to make a sweater, the yarns and gauge of those yarns influence light or heavy the final product will be. The fibers are spun into yarns, which are then knit together to form a sweater. The gauge refers to the thickness of those yarns and can be the difference between an airy spring sweater and a chunky deep-winter cardigan. The thicker the gauge, the heavier and warmer the sweater will be.

The balance between material and fabric weight is a delicate one. So when you’re deciding on a sweater, remember that a heavy cotton sweater can potentially be just as warm as a thin merino wool sweater or that a densely knit cashmere sweater will be warmer than an equally chunky cotton alternative.

Recent findings suggest that aside from the rarer summer knitwear, sweaters are made for cold weather. So fit is especially important considering you’ll be layering your sweater over and under other garments. Consider whether you’ll be wearing it over a button-up and tie or just a simple T-shirt. For the slightly reckless, slightly sexier among us, also consider whether you’ll be wearing it without any undershirt at all.

It has been revealed that same goes for the outer layers that’ll go on top. A chunky sweater is satisfying and cozy as hell, but can easily become unwieldy if you’re trying to stuff it under a tailored blazer. When it comes to fit, there’s no single best silhouette, but there are a couple of rules of thumb if you can’t make heads or tails of it. Make sure the shoulder seams hit just past your shoulder bones, that the sleeves reach to your wrist bones, and that the hem sits right around your hips.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “The first rule of acting is that you don’t judge your character,” Julia Garner told an enthralled audience on Thursday evening at Manhattan’s Paris Theater, moments after the credits rolled following the world premiere of The Altruists. The Netflix original series, available on the streaming platform now, sees Garner step into the shoes of Caroline Ellison, the disgraced co-CEO of Alameda Research and on-again, off-again girlfriend of FTX co-founder Sam Bankman-Fried. “I wasn’t necessarily thinking of the fraud. I just wanted people to be able to understand her,” she added.

It has been revealed that after a screening of the surprisingly humorous pilot episode, Garner and her co-star, Anthony Boyle, joined the show’s creator, Graham Moore, for a panel discussion with actor-turned-journalist Ben McKenzie about the treachery, trickery, and turbulence that pervade the world of cryptocurrency. “You’re probably wondering what’s Ryan Atwood doing up here,” McKenzie joked from the stage, referring to his early-aughts turn as one of The O.C.’s leading teen heartthrobs. “For the last four years, I’ve been investigating and documenting fraud and other criminal activity… And having met and interviewed the real Sam Bankman-Fried, I would like to say that Anthony has a lot more charm [than him].”.

The series doesn’t just chronicle the shocking fall of Bankman-Fried and FTX. Rather, it centers largely on the romantic trajectory of the two financial-industry protégés. “It’s the story of two people who I genuinely, to the core of my being, believe got into this for the right reasons and wanted to do the right thing,” Moore said. “But over the course of their tortuous relationship and those six years, they turned each other into people who did the exact opposite of the thing they initially set out to do.” (Drawing a laugh from the crowd, Northern Irish actor Boyle likened their dynamic to “something from an episode of Love on the Spectrum.”).

After the panel, Garner, in a custom ballet-slipper-pink jumpsuit by Haider Ackermann for Tom Ford and an earful of Lorraine Schwartz bling, and an all-black-clad Boyle joined their castmates, crew members, and press for an after-party in The Plaza Hotel’s Oak Room—making it one of the last industry events to be hosted in the storied venue before it closes for a four-year renovation.

Over mini-umbrella-adorned mai-tais and passed bites, guests discussed the show and compared notes on how much they actually understood crypto terminology, while twirling SBF-approved fidget spinners and branded poker chips around in their hands.

Fashion Has Moved Beyond the Runway and Into the Director’s Chair

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that when guests, including Rocky and Qualley, arrived at the show, the story continued where the film had left off.
  • According to recent reports, fashion’s love affair with the silver screen stretches across decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ahead of Matthieu Blazy’s first Chanel Métiers d’art show, Michel Gondry introduced the collection’s world through a surreal short starring Margaret Qualley and A$AP Rocky. Released as a prelude to the runway, the film follows the couple as they drift through New York along parallel paths before finding each other again on a downtown sidewalk, where Rocky proposes moments before they disappear into the subway station together.

Industry observers note that when guests, including Rocky and Qualley, arrived at the show, the story continued where the film had left off. Bhavitha Mandava emerged in silk “jeans,” followed later by Mona Tougaard, Anok Yai, and Alex Consani, each embodying a different New York archetype, from the sharply tailored power executive to the impeccably dressed society woman. As they moved through the decommissioned station at Bowery and Kenmare Street in Blazy’s reimagined tweeds, the everyday commute took on a cinematic quality. “Designers are directors themselves, except we’re all their actors,” claims Jane Rosenthal, an Academy Award-nominated producer, co-founder of the Tribeca Festival, and co-chair of the board of Tribeca Enterprises. “When they create characters this vivid, they’re creating not just a dress, but a feeling people want to inhabit.”.

According to recent reports, fashion’s love affair with the silver screen stretches across decades. Coco Chanel designed costumes for two Jean Renoir films; Hubert de Givenchy created Audrey Hepburn’s black sheath dress for Breakfast at Tiffany’s. Today, the relationship runs in both directions. Julian Klausner’s spring/summer 2027 collection for Dries Van Noten borrowed the language of cinema through imagined movie posters splashed on slips and party skirts, while the Angelina Jolie-starring Couture turned its attention to the women behind the seams.

And as film culture enjoys a renaissance of its own, fashion is deepening its relationship with the medium. Letterboxd has turned cinephilia into a social, gamified experience, while celebrities now revel in the chance to highlight their most obscure Criterion Collection favorites. Fashion, ever attuned to shifts in culture, has followed suit, moving beyond the familiar fields of costume design and cinematic campaigns to support and sometimes produce filmmaking itself.

In a recent development, since 2015, Through Her Lens: The Tribeca Chanel Women’s Filmmaker Program, co-founded by Rosenthal, has paired mentorship with financial support for emerging female and nonbinary filmmakers. This year’s program brought together mentors such as Celine Song and Gina Prince-Bythewood, who worked directly with participants.

Rosenthal points out that the number of female-directed films has, unfortunately, dipped in recent years. After over a decade of the program, “What we’re finding is that the community is really intentional,” she says. “Our advisory board wants to be here. They come back year after year. They want to be part of it, because they want to help support the next generation.” Miu Miu’s Women’s Tales, established by Miuccia Prada in 2011, has similarly become a platform for female filmmakers—including Ava DuVernay, Claire Denis, and Mona Fastvold—to tell original stories. Those initiatives were early signs of a broader shift.

According to recent reports, in September, Dior announced a two-year creative partnership with A24, the studio behind auteur-driven hits like Marty Supreme and Everything Everywhere All at Once, spanning film, theater, and live events at the Cherry Lane Theatre in Manhattan’s West Village. The collaboration was introduced online with a tongue-in-cheek short directed by Aidan Zamiri, in which Sabrina Carpenter, Josh O’Connor, and Drew Starkey auditioned to play Dior creative director Jonathan Anderson. (The announcement kicked off with a companion teaser, featuring Carpenter dressed as Anderson himself, complete with his now instantly recognizable formula of a plaid shirt, jeans, and Salomons.).

It has been revealed that under its former creative director Anthony Vaccarello, Saint Laurent debuted Saint Laurent Productions in 2023, backing acclaimed films including Pedro Almodóvar’s Strange Way of Life and Jacques Audiard’s Oscar-winning melodrama Emilia Pérez. And Rolex has also invested in cinema’s future, supporting the Student Academy Awards, which platform emerging filmmakers, partnering with festivals like the New York Film Festival and the Sundance Institute as an official partner and exclusive timepiece, and serving as a founding supporter of the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures.

It has been revealed that tara Maria Gonzalez, a fashion writer and author of the Substack newsletter Cult Classic, notes that film allows brands room to build worlds rather than simply present collections or have their designs live in the endless scroll of social media. “People are growing tired of seeing the same trends,” she explains. “It’s like, ‘Well, why do I need to buy that if everybody else has it?’ When designers align themselves with directors, that adds a level of depth that can also connect to a wider audience.”.

Industry observers note that look no further than Balenciaga, which enlisted Past Lives and Materialists director Song to helm the short film A Fresh York Minute. Song built a character study around Sarah Pidgeon, using Pierpaolo Piccioli’s designs as a narrative thread rather than the main attraction. It leaves the viewer to focus on a mood before a product, an inversion of what fashion advertising has traditionally asked us to do. “Brands are [showing] that fashion isn’t just for people who self-identify as ‘fashion people,’” Gonzalez notes. “Fashion has the mass appeal that can speak to anybody who’s interested in storytelling. And one of the most accessible forms of storytellingis film.”.

Recent findings suggest that like Gondry’s lovers disappearing into the subway station, the most memorable fashion stories don’t end when the collection arrives on the runway or on the shop floor. They only become more interesting out on the streets, where clothes become characters and the city becomes the set.

#88986. “Two Girls Who Speak All the Time About Politics”: Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira Take On Capitalism in All of a Sudden

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1835 w)

“Two Girls Who Speak All the Time About Politics”: Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira Take On Capitalism in All of a Sudden

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we’re all seeking comfort as the world ends.
  • All of a Sudden tells the story of two women who forge a formidable friendship as they face personal and professional hardship.
  • The film is an adaptation of a nonfiction book, When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher With Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist, which collects correspondence from two Japanese-speaking academics as they reflect on health care and death during the last few months of philosopher Makiko Miyano’s life (who inspired Okamoto’s character).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we’re all seeking comfort as the world ends. Environmental, economic, and political pressures weigh heavily on our minds as tangible solutions feel farther and farther out of reach. Solace is a rare commodity in a world controlled by unrelenting capitalist forces. In All of a Sudden, filmmaker Ryusuke Hamaguchi suggests that as we face tragedy, we must remember our vital need for human connection.

All of a Sudden tells the story of two women who forge a formidable friendship as they face personal and professional hardship. Marie-Lou Fontaine (Virginie Efira) runs an elder-care facility near Paris, where she introduces a “Humanitude” methodology designed to treat patients with dignity and introduce listening-heavy caretaking practice. She befriends Mari (Tao Okamoto), a terminally ill theater director from Japan. Ryusuke chronicles this relationship through extended, emotional conversations, spoken in both Japanese and French, and covering topics from identity to mortality.

The film is an adaptation of a nonfiction book, When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher With Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist, which collects correspondence from two Japanese-speaking academics as they reflect on health care and death during the last few months of philosopher Makiko Miyano’s life (who inspired Okamoto’s character). Instead of keeping the fact that the two pen pals spoke the same language, he introduced French and moved the story to Paris. This small change forced the story to confront language gaps, exploring the power of conversation and listening and asserting that so much can be achieved through this mediation.

Efira and Okamoto understand their characters’ simmering anxieties and outlooks on the world, providing the bedrock for these impressively naturalistic performances. The two actresses sustain long, philosophical conversation with such intensity throughout the entire three hours and 16 minutes. In a rare occurrence, the two shared the Best Actress Award at the Cannes Film Festival, where the movie premiered this summer. In the film, their budding friendship serves as a sounding board for each other, as Marie-Lou grapples with the pressure of capitalism on her medical staff and Mari comes to terms with the end of her life. In typical fashion, Ryusuke lets the camera linger on these two actresses during these prolonged philosophical interactions, forcing the audience to sit with the gravity of their situations.

Ahead of the theatrical release of Ryusuke’s latest feature film, Bazaar spoke to Efira and Okamoto about the first time they read the script, how they built an intimate bond despite speaking two different languages, and the punk, anti-capitalist edge fueling this intimate, conversation-heavy film.

In a recent development, tao Okamoto: It’s the scene where she talks about capitalism while writing on the whiteboard. That’s one of the strangest scenes in the movie. I felt connected to the character because I am also a climate activist myself. I’ve been spreading the word about climate crises on podcasts, and I talk about it daily. When I read the part, I felt, “I need to play this character.”.

Sources indicate that virginie Efira: It’s the same for me, because this scene is so special. When I read it, the movie felt like one of the most profound, special, and radical readings. You have two girls who speak all the time about politics. We don’t see that. I never see that in other movies. Sometimes, when a director wants to put something philosophical, political, or intellectual, they say, “Maybe we’ll do three minutes,” otherwise the audience will be bored. No, this movie spent 15 minutes [discussing capitalism], and I remarked, “Oh yes, that’s so punk!” The film has its own language. When I read All of a Sudden, I could hear the language of the movie, and I wanted to approach it. When I met Tao, I thought, “Oh, we are so lucky to be an actress and work with [Ryusuke], but also to share this material with him.”.

According to recent reports, VE: I only knew one word in Japanese before making the movie. Then, to be able to speak Japanese at a high level, because the character studied in Japan, I must first learn to read, then learn to embody the language. Finding the language of the movie was strange. There’s a flat and natural way to play [in one of Ryusuke’s movies]. He spoke to me about Cassavetes and Gena Rowlands, but also about Bresson. Neutral performances. You find it when you open up, and when I opened to Tao, we discovered the right language for the movie. We did a lot of flat readings before shooting. We never rehearsed in motion, so when we finally performed for the first time, we awakened the text.

In a recent development, TO: I’m going to add that because I started my career in America, finding a middle ground by using a language that’s not my mother tongue is normal for me. On the surface, that part wasn’t a challenge for me. Finding the language for this film and respecting Hamaguchi’s way of working were priorities. We were naturally drawn to his talent and wanted to make his dream happen and be part of it.

TO: I joined this project way after Virginie. I luckily had months to prepare with him, and during rehearsals, you drop all emotion and read the text as if you were reading numbers. On top of that, I got to visit some institutes, such as the Cancer Research Center and places where people work with disabled people, to build up my understanding of my role’s point of view. Reading the text over and over was a unique experience for me. [Ryusuke] can really listen to the actor’s voice and tell the difference between someone who is simply reading and someone really concentrating. Even though you’re not supposed to put any emotions, you have to be present; you have to be there. I’ve never experienced such rich, profound preparation for a role.

Industry observers note that VE: We shot in a real nursing home. There was a mix between fiction and reality. Sometimes filmmaking becomes standardized, with no room left to breathe, but with Hamaguchi, you’re sure he will leave room for the unexpected and for uncertainty. It allows you to embrace the unpredictability of reality. He’s not looking for an accident, but for the ability to be in the present. A viewer of Hamaguchi’s work will always feel a sensation of documentation, but it’s still always cinema. To be an actor in his movies is to be naturalistic, to be in the present, to capture some details and really embrace this unpredictability. The filming process becomes an adventure he wants you to have. One day, he told me, “I hope that you will find the light.” He said a lot of cryptic things. He said to me, “Don’t use your text like a tool; just go inside the text.”.

In a recent development, TO: The script is already amazing. And I could read it over and over again, and that was a joy. But he mentioned that I should read the original book. It’s about two women exchanging letters—or emails. They are real people who the characters are modeled after. I wanted to please the people who know these women, not to make them too different from them. I first put pressure on myself to portray this woman as close to the real person, but it was impossible for me because this person passed away in 2019. I couldn’t do much research, so I interviewed her mother and the co-writer. That provided me with a lot of clues, but reading their exchanged letters already gave me the soul of this movie.

It has been revealed that VE: He gives the book to the actresses, but also to the entire team. I never felt something so collective, and you will feel it in the movie, from the sound engineer to someone who only stayed two days on set. I also met the anthropologist. When you read this book, it’s full of life. It gives you a perceptible beauty of things. The book has a kind of energy; it helps you keep a level of optimism even when you know the situation is hopeless. In this book, it speaks about what it’s like to be alive. Maybe there’s beauty in life because we are going to die.

Industry observers note that TO: For me, I came on this project at the last minute, only a month before. Virginie was so dedicated to studying Japanese from scratch; it was so impressive how she studied all this writing, reading, and lines. Seeing that, I had a huge admiration, like “Who can do this!?” As you can see, Virginie’s so charming; nobody would hate her. It was so easy for me to be drawn to her as a person, as the characters in the movie were discovering each other.

VE: We got to know each other through the shoot. I was happy not to know much at the beginning and to progressively get deeper into our relationship. We lived all that together. I conflate Marie-Lou’s feelings for Mari with Virginie’s feelings for Tao, because we share that. It will be an end, not a tragic one like in the movie, but it will be an end. But I know Tao will carry this experience in her heart forever, and I will too. He let us feel what we want to feel.

In a recent development, TO: I study environmental issues, and I always thought capitalism is responsible for our world’s issues. Something I didn’t know until I read this script was that capitalism doesn’t only exploit our environment, but also our human bodies—human labor and our time. When I connected those dots, I realized all the problems could be blamed on capitalism. We’re looking for time and looking for happiness—or security—and all these things can be related to a capitalistic way of living. I think it’s great that Hamaguchi connected that fundamental issue to Marie-Lou’s situation in the elderly home. She’s frustrated, as is Marie. She’s battling her cancer, and it can be connected to this economic issue.

In a recent development, VE: Cinema can show bodies, fatigue, and with Marie-Lou, you see a certain fatigue because capitalism creates it. How do we deal with that? We say, “Oh, capitalism’s not good. We don’t have time. And we want to be richer and richer.” But how do we fight that, because everything is already there? I come from France, and you see all the young people outside. The real question is, what can cinema do with that? It’s not a theoretical thing, but Hamaguchi can find a solution. It’s speaking, listening to the other, sharing ideas; it’s movement. If I look for a solution to this problem with money, I’ll remain a prisoner of this way of functioning. Even if you think you’re not in a stage of capitalism, you are.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the one thing that can make classic apple pie better?
  • Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers.
  • 2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

According to recent reports, make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Industry observers note that turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

It has been revealed that do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

According to recent reports, place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

According to recent reports, add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

In a recent development, stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Industry observers note that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

It has been revealed that place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

Industry News: Doing Crime Barely Covers My Menswear Habit in GTA VI

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1381 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I am still slightly delirious.
  • It has been revealed that most people will have spent their first-ever session getting through the missions, exploring the map, and finding out what Jason and Lucia have got themselves into.
  • According to recent reports, before we get into it, you should know: Your in-game clothes matter more than ever compared to other entries in the Grand Theft Auto universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I am still slightly delirious. When GTA 6 came out at midnight last week, I played it for eight hours straight, all in the name of real, boots-on-the-ground journalism. Well, there was a quick power nap somewhere around 5 a.m., but otherwise I've been working very hard. I have a new wardrobe and some concerns about the price of digital jorts.

It has been revealed that most people will have spent their first-ever session getting through the missions, exploring the map, and finding out what Jason and Lucia have got themselves into. Not me. My main goal was to visit as many shops as possible. It's been 13 years since GTA 5; I wanted to see what had happened to the menswear.

According to recent reports, before we get into it, you should know: Your in-game clothes matter more than ever compared to other entries in the Grand Theft Auto universe. As I wrote last week, the new “heat” system lets cops remember what you were wearing, so losing them doesn't necessarily mean you're in the clear. Changing your hat or sunglasses won't clear the clothing clue, either. You need a full fit change. So technically, all this shopping could help me get away with something. That's my justification, anyway.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, even virtual shopping requires cold, hard cash—and early on, that takes considerably more effort than I'd hoped. You start with almost nothing, spending much of the opening stretch around Key Lento in swampy Mariana County. I'd gone in expecting to buy loads of clothes. Instead, I was checking what I could afford.

My first opportunity came in a random gun shop that also sold some workwear. I had a quick browse then went straight for the camo shorts. Back in August, British GQ's senior style editor Mahalia Chang declared that “camo shorts are fucking back, baby,” having watched Jason spend much of the trailer wearing them. Who was I to argue?

According to recent reports, nearby, in Hamlet, I found a few thrift shops and picked up a battered chore jacket with more than a little Carhartt Detroit about it. It looked properly used, which suited both my budget and the general condition of my pickup. I bought a watch, too, but more on that another time.

I was already getting quite into it. I was comparing pieces, checking prices, and deciding what could wait. There were clothes I wanted and clothes I could afford. Annoyingly, the game understood the difference.

I bought a trucker cap at one point and was very happy with it. Over the summer, I wrote about wanting to give them another go despite having a head my mates call “a sniper's dream.” Jason doesn't have that problem (in a metaphorical sense, anyway), so I thought I'd let him enjoy one. Shortly afterwards, a gang of lads picked a fight with me, punched me, and knocked it off his head. I fled, only realizing once I was safely away that I hadn't picked it back up. I'd barely had a chance to enjoy it. I hope one of them's wearing it at least.

After a few missions, I finally had enough money to justify another shopping trip. I got into my beaten-up pickup and headed downtown, where the prices started getting a little more serious. Denim jackets were around $120. A pair of dark wash jorts I really liked cost $45, which was slightly more than I wanted to spend.

I appreciate that this is a game in which you can steal a car, and I was still having a small financial discussion with myself about the price of shorts. For a game called Grand Theft Auto, I'd done surprisingly little car stealing in the time I'd been playing.

The map is absolutely massive, and there almost 70 clothing stores to work through, so visiting everything was never gonna happen in one sitting. Cars now use fuel, too. Driving miles out of your way to look at a jacket comes with an additional expense, and I had to leave enough money to get home.

There was a reason to keep exploring, though. I went into another shop expecting more of the same and realized the stock was different, so now I wanted to check the other shops before buying anything. Apparently, I'd waited 13 years to recreate how I spend my Saturdays.

Naturally, I decided to drive to Ocean Beach, a more expensive part of the city where I had very little business shopping. Inside Nola, the person at the till looked me up and down in my shitty workwear and asked, “Eh, are you looking for somebody?”.

It was an impressively efficient assessment of my finances. Nola felt a little like Casablanca, the French-Moroccan label known for colorful prints, sportswear, and clothes that suggest a considerably nicer holiday than the one you're on. I'd previously called Hawaiian shirts “the unofficial uniform of Vice City.” Here, joining in cost about $330. Blazers were about $430. I could look, provided I didn't get any dirt on anything.

Industry observers note that then I accidentally punched the shop assistant; I'm still getting used to the controls. At least, I think it was an accident. Either way, I had to flee before I could give the blazers much consideration. When I came back later, the store was temporarily closed. I hope it wasn't due to staff injuries.

Other boutiques were even less accommodating to my balance. Italian house Ferruccio Tucci (probably a GTA-ified Emilio Pucci) had $3,000 suits and $1,200 horsebit loafers. I went in to browse and accidentally bought a pair of $350 shades, which was a very expensive way to learn which button does what. The annoying thing is that they looked genuinely sick—exactly the sort of thing I'd wear IRL, which made it much easier to justify keeping them. Well, that was fuel and dinner gone for the day. At least I could look good while walking home.

Sources indicate that later, driving past Waxman Island, I came across Vice City's Eris flagship. Obviously, I had to go in. For anyone who hasn't spent the past few months staring at fictional trainers, Eris is basically GTA's answer to Nike. Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory; Eris is the goddess of strife and discord. The shoes are often just as recognizable as the joke.

Recent findings suggest that the store kinda reminded me a little of Niketown in London—right now closed for refurbishment—with neon lights and big statues and enough footwear to keep me occupied considerably longer than was sensible. There was the Rise Low, an Air Force 1 lookalike that I ended up getting in two colourways; the Strife 360, with its very Air Max 97-ish shape; and the Rook 1 High, which follows the Air Jordan 1 High. I own more than 400 pairs of sneakers IRL—I probably should've known that going in here would be a problem.

And Eris is only one option. There are alternative sneaker labels, beach shops, souvenir shops, and smaller, DIY-looking streetwear brands all dotted around the city. I'd barely begun working through them. Every time I thought I'd seen enough to stop, there was another shop worth going into.

The most expensive-looking thing I acquired didn't come from a boutique at all. Slight spoiler: A naked man offered to give me his “Crowex” watch after pulling a plastic egg out of his own ass. (Yes, you read that right.) You'll know him when you see him. I'm not gonna go into any more detail, partly because I'm tired and partly because I'd like you to experience that transaction yourself.

Eight hours in, I'd hardly scratched the surface. What surprised me most was how long the expensive stuff felt like it would take to earn. Those suits and loafers were sitting there, available to try, while my balance suggested another few missions first. There's a lot of city left to explore, quite a few shops I want to revisit, and a pair of jorts I'm still thinking about.

For now, though, I need some sleep. And Jason needs to earn back that $350.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

It started out as an otherwise happy moment for me. I was attending the historic inauguration of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and celebrating the first Muslim mayor in Upcoming York City’s history. It was an occasion being celebrated by not just New Yorkers but also fellow Americans and people around the world for the symbol of increasing visibility and inclusion that the moment represented for so many of us. In the selfie, I’m bundled up in a burgundy fur-trimmed coat, my hijab clinging to my head against the cold winter wind. I’m proudly smiling at the camera. Despite the cold, I’m so happy. It was this photo, uploaded to my X account, that users prompted Grok to regenerate in rapid succession in ways that violated my consent and religious autonomy. They used an AI chatbot to digitally take control of my body to inflict their abuse.

“I’ve always wondered what you all whackos look like without all that mess.”.

I founded Muslim Girl, a digital media platform, as a teenager to reclaim our narratives and identities online. I wanted Muslim women to speak for ourselves, on our own terms, instead of allowing others to define us. I’ve dedicated my career to empowering women to take control of their own choices. But in a matter of moments, Grok robbed me of mine.

Industry observers note that elon Musk, the owner of xAI, essentially removed all the guardrails from Grok to compete in the AI race. By allowing Grok’s image generation feature to remove clothing and promote its “spicy” capabilities, Musk was banking on consumers using it for sexual purposes without any regard to the harms it would cause.

Sources indicate that the person I was most afraid to tell was my dad. After my mom passed away a few years ago, he’s become way more protective of his only daughter, and for an old-school Arab Muslim immigrant, I didn’t know how he would react. He was furious. At first, I was afraid he was going to be mad at me for being in this situation since I have always been a vocally public woman online. But he understood very quickly that technology was being used to inflict the same abuse I had gotten used to online in more advanced and extreme ways.

It has been revealed that most of my elders don’t know the difference between AI-generated images and real photos, especially those who habitually forward chain messages in massive WhatsApp family group chats. My dad had to figure out a way to preemptively and sensitively explain to them what happened. Even though the images weren’t technically real, the humiliation of having to explain them to family and friends remained the same.

Coming from a religiously conservative background heightened the feeling of violation I experienced. The hijab is meant to be a woman’s choice. I’ve worn mine since I was 13 years old, so no public photos of me exist without me wearing it. I wear the hijab not out of heightened strictness or chastity, but rather as a guard against the male gaze in a hypersexualized society that commodifies women’s bodies and pressures us into how we should look or present ourselves.

Once the choice to cover or uncover is taken from a woman, it can easily become a tool of control and dominance over her body. In France, we’ve seen the proposal of a hijab ban that would fine women for covering, at the same time as we’ve watched countries like Afghanistan force women to cover. In all cases, the point is asserting power over women’s bodies.

According to recent reports, technology has created new ways to violate our autonomy while our current laws struggle to keep pace with protecting our rights in the AI era. Our bodies are still a battleground. Only now, the battleground is digital.

When the notifications started pouring in, I didn’t know what to do against the faceless mob that was using Grok to replicate and violate my identity in such shocking ways. I called the police, and when they came over, I had to endure the first humiliating experience of showing them the photos. They took a police report, said there was nothing they could do, and suggested that I make my account private. I refuse to diminish myself from the public at risk of having my basic rights and dignity violated online. None of us should have to.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why I’m suing Elon Musk’s xAI. This isn’t just about my hijab or even about me. It’s about what we will and will not allow AI to do to us. I hope this becomes a landmark case that draws a line for the rights we are entitled to online. Even if it means standing up to the richest man on Earth.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that without fail, the eyes are usually the first place a busy week (or month) shows up. A late night, skipping your skin-care routine, or long flight easily translates to a little puffiness in the morning or some shadowing underneath, and maybe even the dreaded “eye bag.” It happens to everyone, and it usually fades once you’ve caught up on sleep, gotten back on your regimen, and have hydrated enough.

According to recent reports, some of it comes down to how the area is built. The skin around the eyes is thinner than on the rest of the face, so whatever’s going on underneath, like fluid that settled overnight or tiny blood vessels close to the surface, is easier to see. Over time, collagen gradually decreases and the brows can sit a touch lower, which is a completely normal part of getting older. Still, it’s nice to have a few tricks for the days you want to look as awake as you feel.

The good news? There are plenty of ways we can brighten, lift, and hydrate this area of the face. Some are as easy as curling your lashes or keeping a couple of spoons in the freezer. Other methods, like an eye cream with studied ingredients, work slowly over a few months after a little consistency. If you want to go further, in-office treatments can subtly lift the brow or soften dark circles. Below, our experts share their best tips for brightening and lifting the eye area, starting with the simplest.

Recent findings suggest that makeup artist Lynsey Alexander has transformed many a tired eye in her time, having worked with models backstage at fashion reveals and on shoots for years. She always begins with good eye drops. “I then use a beige pencil secretly inside the eyes–it needs to be a skin-toned color, white is too stark,” she notes. “My favorite is from Paris Berlin as it’s quite dry and not overly creamy, something you don’t want as it moves too easily.”.

“Dark circles are a common complaint in my office,” says aesthetic doctor, Maryam Zamani, MD. “One of the most common reasons for dark circles is loss of volume in the periorbital area. As we age, the eyelid-cheek junction becomes elongated, and where this junction was once confluent in youth, it becomes demarcated, giving the appearance of dark lower eyelids or tear troughs.” It’s a common problem that can begin from as early as your twenties, and is made worse as collagen stores deplete. Dr. Zamani often treats it with “meticulously placed micro-droplets of hyaluronic acid” to restore the lost volume and hydrate. You will see brighter, more awake eyes immediately.

Celebrity makeup artist Mary Phillips has prepped clients like Hailey Bieber and Kendall Jenner for years, and she knows tired eyes are usually the first thing to give a face away. Her fix starts with a step she has coined called underglazing. “The under-eye area is one of the first places I focus on when prepping the skin because it’s so delicate, and can show dryness and fine lines more easily,” she claims. “‘Underglazing’ is really about giving that area the hydration it needs before applying any makeup. I love using lightweight, hydrating skin care and gently pressing it into the skin to help everything absorb. The goal is to make the skin look naturally plump and hydrated, so you need less makeup to begin with.”.

In a recent development, the newly introduced wave of the best eye creams are more effective than ever before, and come loaded with efficacious active ingredients to illuminate the area and soften fine lines, while maintaining the integrity of the skin barrier. “Tretinoin has the best evidence behind it–with continued use (for about a year), you see increased cell turnover; cue brightening of the skin and a reduction in wrinkles,” explains dermatologist Emma Craythorne, MD. “Azelaic acid is also brilliant at brightening, if used in strength at five per cent.”.

Sources indicate that if your problem is puffiness, take care to ensure you opt for a detoxifying eye cream instead of a hydrating formula–according to Dr. Zamani, hydrating eye creams (particularly those with hyaluronic acid) may exacerbate it.

Yes, it’s boring, but what you eat and drink does make a massive difference to the eye area. Those who have ever woken up the morning after with eyes that feel like lead will know that. “Keeping salt and alcohol low in your diet is key,” says Dr, Zamani. “And sleeping with a pillow and eye mask can also help.”.

To stimulate the area and help de-puff, facialist Nichola Joss recommends gently massaging an eye cream or gel around the outer orbital bone. “You can also use cold teaspoons to gently stimulate, de-puff, improve lymph drainage and brighten the area,” she says. For those more serious about texture and pigmentation, she also recommends the Lyma Laser, which can be used at home.

Turns out there are a lot of veins and capillaries underneath delicate, thin skin in the eye area, which can cause the dark hue we recognize as dark circles. “We can use sophisticated lasers to target the vascular plexus in the upper and lower eyelid,” claims aesthetic surgeon, Costas Papageorgiou, MD, who works from Harrods Wellness Clinic in London. “This plexus tends to become more prominent with age as a result of accumulative inflammation and loss of elasticity, to name two.” By addressing (and softening) this area, you can reinstate skin clarity and light reflection–plus it works particularly well when combined with under eye filler.

To address cool tones and general darkness in the area, try color correcting. “For blue undertones, opt for a peach-based concealer,” advises Dr. Alexander, who also adds a touch of YSL’s cult Touche Eclat to reflect light in the area. “Then, set the under eyes with a brightening powder, such as Laura Mercier’s Secret Brightening Powder, for added radiance.”.

Simple but effective, curling your eyelashes has an immediate refreshing effect. “Creating a bright, lifted eye is about creating space between the brow and lash line, and drawing attention outwards and upwards,” explains Anna Payne, UK Chanel makeup artist. For a little extra oomph, she suggests applying a dot of highlighting shadow on the centre of the eyelid and inner corner of the eye to create an illuminating spotlight effect.

When we analyze drooping or lackluster eyes, we don’t often consider that part of the problem might be coming from the forehead. “One of the biggest reasons that the eye area looks tired is that on top of the tiny repetitive blinking movements our eyes have to do each day, we also express an array of emotions through them, too,” notes Ada Ooi, TCM practitioner and founder of 001 Skincare. “A lot of our eye movements, such as frowning or surprise, come from muscles in the forehead.” She recommends using a gua sha tool to alleviate the tension built in the frontalis muscles (the vertical muscles that lift the brows). Try cross-friction massage (horizontally, in this case) to break them from their usual position, and release fascia stress.

Sources indicate that “Freshly threaded brows have transformational powers,” sys Vanita Parti MBE, founder of Blink Brow Bar. “By de-fluffing, removing excess stragglers and creating two neat, symmetrical brows, you open up the eyes immediately.” Lifting the arch also lifts and sculpts the entire face, so post-thread, seek to define them with a brow pencil or pomade.

In a recent development, if curling your lashes is already part of your morning, think of this as the version that lasts. Lash lift technician and founder of beauty studio Studio.Lbb recommends it to anyone who’d rather skip the curler altogether. “A lash lift enhances your natural lashes by lifting, curling and tinting them for a longer, darker and more defined look—without extensions or mascara,” she says. Results usually last six to eight weeks, so it’s a smart one to book before a vacation or a stretch of early mornings.

According to recent reports, for a quick lift without needles, celebrity facialist and founder of M.A.S.C. Studio Alessandro Cirino points to microcurrent, which sends low-level electrical currents through the skin to wake up the muscles underneath. “Microcurrent can help tone and firm the eye contour, for a fresher-looking result,” he adds. As for a permanent result, Cirino claims the research is still limited. Think of it more as a refresh before a big day unless you keep up with a daily routine.

It has been revealed that most people think of crow’s feet when it comes to injectables around the eyes, but the brow is the less obvious spot for injection. “When strategically placed, neuromodulators can subtly elevate the outer brow by relaxing the muscles responsible for pulling it downward,” notes Dr. Casey Goodman, medical director of TIEV. “In the right patient, even a slight elevation can make the eyes appear more open, rested, and refreshed.” Dosing matters more here than almost anywhere else on the face. “Overcorrecting can compromise natural expression or even create heaviness where we intended to create lift,” Goodman says. “The goal isn’t to make someone look treated. It’s to make them look like themselves, without the subtle signs of fatigue that may not reflect how they actually feel.”.

Recent findings suggest that when we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue's vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry's standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to brightening and lifting treatments, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: modality, ingredients, texture, packaging, finish, and the skin-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you. Read more about our testing methodology here.

Other stars who were present included actors from Netflix’s The Body, like Sofia Wylie and Emily Roman, alongside musicians like Jade, reality stars like Melanie Moreno, and more.

No matter what happens professionally, it’s clear that these young women will continue to show up for each another as friends.

Industry News: The Real-Life Wardrobe of Michael Bennett, Who Traded the NFL for Furniture Design

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
