💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you’ve won a Super Bowl ring, made three Pro Bowl appearances, and played a key role on one of the most dominant defensive squads ever—the Seattle Seahawks’ 2010s-era Legion of Boom—what do you do next?
  • Sources indicate that after completing his 11-year NFL career in 2020, the 41-year-old enrolled at two institutions—the University of Hawaii and Seattle’s Heritage School of Interior Design—to study architecture and interior design, respectively.
  • Recent findings suggest that all that effort is paying off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you’ve won a Super Bowl ring, made three Pro Bowl appearances, and played a key role on one of the most dominant defensive squads ever—the Seattle Seahawks’ 2010s-era Legion of Boom—what do you do next? For Michael Bennett, the answer was to head back to school.

Sources indicate that after completing his 11-year NFL career in 2020, the 41-year-old enrolled at two institutions—the University of Hawaii and Seattle’s Heritage School of Interior Design—to study architecture and interior design, respectively. “I’m a student of whatever I do,” Bennett tells me. “My best quality—and probably my worst quality—is that the things I love to do, I try to become the best. I play tennis five days a week. I’m trying to go to Wimbledon. And design and architecture are like that.”.

Recent findings suggest that all that effort is paying off. Through his design practice Studio Kër, Bennett debuted an 11-piece collection of avant-garde furniture inspired by the African diaspora in 2024, which was well received by critics. He’s now hard at work on his sophomore line, alongside a spoken-word album and the occasional bespoke garment.

It has been revealed that that last side quest should come as no surprise, because Bennett has some of the most distinctive personal style I’ve ever seen on a pro athlete–current or former—with a particularly clean headwear and accessories game. Here, Bennett tells me all about the skills he carried over from football into his new career, what fatherhood has taught him about masculinity, and the song he listens to every day.

According to recent reports, michael Bennett: I’ve been playing football my whole life, man. After winning so much, I dug deep. I had already conquered the body. How do I conquer the mind? At what point am I being selfish? I’m missing so much of my kids’ lives. I’ve already been to the highest of the high. Am I going to leave my family with a broken man? That was really the question. Am I chasing ego or am I chasing something else? In reality, a lot of us are just chasing the ego, to be remembered, scared of the death of what [your life] was rather than [embracing] the growth that can be.

Recent findings suggest that people want to keep others in a certain box because that’s the way that they understand them. That’s in any relationship. If you started to date somebody when they’re 20 and you turn 40 and they start to change, you’d be like, “You used to like your eggs like that.” People don’t allow others to transition; won’t allow people to actually experience growth. Often you’re meeting people in a time where they’re just starting to learn who they are. Over time you start to really develop who you are.

In a recent development, the truth is it doesn’t matter if people take you seriously, [as long as] you take yourself seriously. What are you doing to practice your craft? Artists are like, “Oh, my practice, my practice.” I never really understood what that meant until I started doing my own practice. I practiced on the field and I can practice the body. But really, if you want to be taken seriously intellectually, then you have to practice the mind. Sometimes practicing the mind is also connected to the body. In football, yeah, you are connected to the mind in a certain way. But it isn’t always like learning to be a lawyer or an architect or an artist—to be a thinker, you’re doing something completely different. And it’s just allowing yourself to transition. Man, truthfully, you got to say fuck everybody.

According to recent reports, I think it’s one of the most intellectual sports in general. Tennis is one of those sports where it’s about the angle, the quick twitch. You’re by yourself. With football, it’s the amount of moving parts. People overlook the amount of detail that it takes to run a team—practicing and going through a play 3,000 times before you actually get it. The best players I ever met were the smartest when it came to the sport. They were the PhDs of their craft.

Recent findings suggest that it’s taught me vulnerability. It made me a better human. In some ways, my daughters have allowed me to mature. The sport of football requires so much masculinity. I’m not saying that all masculinity is toxic, [but] it’s more about, how do you hunt but still be gentle? The true samurai doesn’t strike, but knows he can.

It has been revealed that what my daughters have allowed me to do is develop my whole humanity. To have a daughter is so special—women are very special. As an athlete, people come back from injuries, but to see a woman come back from giving birth is a whole other level of love. My daughters have been my greatest accomplishments in my life. I never made a Super Bowl trophy. There’s always another winner. But there’s only one Peyton, there’s only one Blake, and there’s one Ollie. As a maker, those are the most special things that I could make.

In 2019, I was really into Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois and [their debate over] the “Talented Tenth.” [Booker T. Washington believed that] intellectualism should never get away from the idea of making. I got into design because I’ve always been involved in politics, and politically, I started to realize that everything came down to design.

Shirt and pants by Studio Kër. Shoes by Collegium.

Whenever I spoke out about police brutality or on critical complications in America, that was really where I started to think about design as this language—this form of resistance. How can I change the system? It starts with design. Where I grew up, a non-gentrified area that was low income, it’s like you could see that there was no empathetic way of thinking about design. The definition of architecture for me is empathy for space. That’s what led me to this idea of these African diaspora forms and languages that I will use as my form of resistance.

I’m working on a newly introduced collection of furniture. The first collection I did was called “We Gotta Get Back to the Crib,” which to me was really about getting back to the essence of Blackness. A lot of times we talk about Blackness and it’s always connected to traumatic experience. But to me, it was more about how can I connect to these true levels of love, these things really shaped my culture, my family, my mother, my grandmother, and everything that was beautiful about being Black? This next collection is about African brutalism. How can I bring these things that are seen in the ghetto in America and in West Africa and then turn those into ideas about furniture? A lot of times what I’m dealing with as a designer is this idea of abstraction. How can I pull and reference something in such a sweet way? Like how Virgil designed shoes with references, leaving crumbs to this unspoken past. As a designer, that’s what I’m trying to do.

Yeah, I got a spoken word project.

According to recent reports, as an athlete, if you talk about your cars or you talk about your jewelry, the way that you gained it doesn’t have that kind of Jay-Z effect—you didn’t hustle to get that. You played to get that, which is different from somebody hustling to get that. With spoken word, I think about Gil Scott-Heron or The Last Poets. They’re talking about critical issues. My perspective is really about humanizing the Black experience and the Black man. My stories and what I’m trying to tell with this music, E-Nigg-Ma, is so much about Black culture, Black design, Black features, this idea of what America is trying to suffocate about Blackness and not let it breathe.

Cuff by Dries van Noten. Ring by Olithica. Watch by Patek Philippe.

In a recent development, music. When I’m designing, beautiful sounds are really notable to the way that I think. My number-one song that I always listen to is Miles Davis’s “Flamenco Sketches.” It’s my daily listen. Those are the sounds that I need to hear: the horn, the riffs, the in-between.

My studio inspires me, just the way light hits. It’s the simplest things. Seeing my family movies. My wife inspires me with what she’s designing.

It has been revealed that my great-grandpa, Hall Mack, everybody talked about his fashion. People still talk about his style. He was the first person I saw dry cleaning everything. His style was impeccable. When I look back at a period of style that I liked, it’d be the years of the Birth of the Cool. People like Miles, Sidney Poitier, everybody was just fresh.

I’ve always been connected to style. People always call me “Runway Mike.” They say, “Bro, you wear more Margiela than anybody I know.” I design my own clothes. [Style] is a part of who you are. I love the idea of fashion. I want to design a fashion show. Yo, Wales Bonner, let me design something for you! I want to be backstage.

Over time I just found me. That takes so much time. I feel like one of the most beautiful things is Instagram and this ability to share things, but one of the worst things is Instagram and the ability to share things. Because there’s a part of us that starts to mimic [what we see] in a way that isn’t true to us. We start to judge ourselves on other people’s experience.

It’s cool to see things, but it’s also cool to experiment with what you feel good in. “Yo, this is what I look good in. I don’t care what nobody claims, I feel good.” That’s what true fashion is. I buy Prada because I actually like it. That’s the development of who you are and your taste—when you buy things for the love of it. Like, “Man, I really love the shoulder on this.” I’m not buying anything to be seen in it. I’m buying it because I respect the process.

Jumpsuit by Studio Kër. Shoes by Prada.

I think it was something from Acne, even though Acne was that middle kind of brand. Acne now has gotten too expensive.

Two things. I bought this striped Prada sweater. It was just a nice, beautiful brown. It was quiet, but it was super nice. And I just designed the blue shirt [from my second look]. Even making something like that is expensive.

I just sketch it, and then I make it in LA.

Yeah, or show a picture of something and break it down like, “Cut this out. I need the arms to be like this.”.

Sources indicate that I’m also going to do it for my studio. My goal is to have studio attire that I produce. This year I’m dropping four shirts. If you’re a designer and you want a beautiful shirt, here’s four of them. I’m only making a hundred of them. Keep it very simple.

It has been revealed that the thing that’s exciting about fashion now is getting away from logos and getting back to beautiful garments. I always loved Issey Miyake, because it’s just so uniform for me. It’s something I wear in the studio all the time—easy to put on, mix and match. It travels well. He was a genius when it came to innovation. A lot of people make clothes, but not a lot of people innovate. I like Wales Bonner. I always like her polo shirts. Margiela and Prada are two of my favorite brands of all time—Prada is just so detailed. Jil Sander is nice. I like Toteme.

Industry observers note that tunnel style is terrible. It’s manufactured. It’s not real. The clothes are wearing them. Half of the things aren’t really who they are. There are some people, like Laremy Tunsil, that are fresh—he’s a big guy from Washington who dresses fresh and it feels like it’s him. But a lot of times you see people that just look like they’re trying too hard to do fashion. Fashion should be quiet and it should be proportioned properly. There’s a geometry to it, and I think that’s what’s missing from tunnel style.

Sources indicate that it’s not the sport, it’s the individual. There are some fresh individuals from each sport that wear dope clothes, like Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. Stefon Diggs. My brother Martellus dresses fresh.

Jay-Z’s 4:44. Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue. And I’m in between Kanye West’s Late Registration and Mos Def & Talib Kweli Are Black Star.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in the days of going to the bookstore at midnight to get a latest book, young fans flocked to their nearest bookstores waiting to see if Katniss Everdeen chose Peeta Mellark or Gale Hawthorne in the hit YA trilogy The Hunger Games. Remember the Borders parties and how many of us would rock a Katniss braid? Those were the days! But the franchise has always been more than a typical young adult series.

From its conception, author Suzanne Collins taught young readers how to have hope in the face of destruction. President Coriolanus Snow wanted the world to fall at his feet and Katniss Everdeen taught audiences to fight back. Still, in the midst of her quest to free the citizens of Panem, a love story was present and it is something that made Suzanne's novels (and the subsequent movies) special.

According to recent reports, the main love triangle of the original run of books and films centered around Katniss Everdeen and her love for both Gale Hawthorne and Peeta Mellark. While the question of who Katniss will choose loomed over the story as our beloved heroes fought for their lives, it felt like the one topic that fans talked about. “Are you Team Peeta or Team Gale?” Unless you were me. I was too busy crying over the death of Finnick Odair and how tragic his love story was. But, still, many of the other fans were focused on why either guy was best for Katniss. That doesn’t mean that was it though. There were other ships that called to us too.

In the middle of all the reapings and rebellions, fans realized one pairing had a different kind of history: Haymitch Abernathy and Effie Trinket. The two never had an explicit romance. Instead, the subtext between Effie and Haymitch led many fans to hope that there was a world where they would find love together. But their first meeting, as seen in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, is not where their will-they-won’t-they love story started. Instead, the prequel taught us more about Haymitch prior to his time in the arena and made it clear that the winner of the second Quarter Quell is one of the franchise’s best love interests.

Industry observers note that this time played by Joseph Zada, fans finally got a glimpse into the love story that broke him. Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak) was a Covey girl, a group of nomadic musicians that fans were first introduced to in the prequel novel and film The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. Haymitch fell in love with her prior to the start of Sunrise on the Reaping, even throwing himself in the line of fire to protect her, leading to him being forced to participate in the second Quarter Quell.

Like many other fans, in the original run of The Hunger Games, I wanted to know about Haymitch’s game. Mainly because we knew he survived by defeating double the amount of tributes that Katniss and Peeta did. It broke something in him. Or so we thought.

Recent findings suggest that during the first trilogy, Haymitch was a drunk, seemingly uncaring about the tributes he was meant to mentor. But I saw something deeper in him, a sadness and loneliness that no one was willing to talk to him about—not that Haymitch would open up anyway. For years, we thought it was the turmoil of the games themselves that sent him into a spiral. Through Sunrise on the Reaping, we got insight into how Haymitch went from a young District 12 boy who actually swore off drinking to the lonely man that Peeta and Katniss encounter during their games. In fact, it’s the same reason why Haymitch actually might be the best love interest in the entire franchise (and yes, that does include the lover boy Finnick Odair himself): His dedication to Lenore Dove.

There is a deep love that all of the characters in The Hunger Games have for their chosen ones. But Haymitch’s dedication to Lenore Dove is rooted in his own grief, loneliness, and fear of hurting someone else he loves.

According to recent reports, president Snow’s continued hatred of District 12 didn’t just reignite with Katniss. Instead, the ripples of his lost romance with Lucy Gray Baird (originally seen in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes) were thrown back in his face when Haymitch tried to break the games he was a part of. It meant that Snow had to send Haymitch a message and he did so in the most devastating way. Snow has Haymitch’s family killed and uses Haymitch’s own gift to Lenore Dove against him. All Haymitch wanted was to protect his family; instead they burn down his house with his family trapped inside and he was forced to hold his one true love in his arms as she died from the poison she unknowingly ingested that was hidden in the candy she thought Haymitch bought her. It’s no wonder why Haymitch isolates himself. He does so so that no one can be hurt by what the Capitol was willing to do to those he loved.

After seeing Sunrise on the Reaping, fans might think that Haymitch is actually more closely related to Finnick Odair in how they both show their love for someone by protecting them in any way possible. Still, Haymitch’s anguish over Lenore Dove kept him alone and separated from the rest of District 12 out of love. Finnick and Mags went into the game during Catching Fire because they both were protecting Annie. Haymitch isolated and drank himself into a stupor for the same reason.

It has been revealed that what can I say? I love two boys who are willing to hurt themselves to keep others safe. And aren’t going to just paint their faces to blend into foliage. (I’m so sorry, Peeta. I do love you, I promise!).

In many ways, Haymitch is the very definition of a “lover boy.” One who loved so deeply that the loss of it changed who he was. Still, the beauty of it shows why Haymitch was so cautious about caring for other people. He wasn’t cold or broken, he was afraid of what President Snow would do to those around him.

Seeing how Haymitch was before the Second Quarter Quell and what he was willing to do for his love of Lenore Dove? It set the standard for what a love interest was willing to do much higher than before. It also means that Peeta Mellark needs to step up his game if he wants to get on Haymitch’s level. “If not for the baby,” isn’t going to cut it when Haymitch is ready to take down an entire empire for love.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this autumn, artists, institutional leaders, collectors, and curators descended on Accra to celebrate a decade of Gallery 1957 and attend Accra Cultural Week, both founded by entrepreneur and art collector Marwan Zakhem.

Since opening in 2016, Gallery 1957 has contributed to the Ghanaian capital’s burgeoning cultural infrastructure. Local artists, Zakhem recalls, “seemed to be doing residencies everywhere” yet they “struggled to make their work here.” So he launched Cultural Week, keen to develop a homegrown creative community while also engaging an international audience. “Cultural Week began because I wanted to bring people to Accra to see what I was seeing.”.

I arrived for the week-long convening at 7 a.m., fresh from the 10-hour flight from New York. As the early morning traffic recalibrated my senses, sights and sounds reminded me of my first visit there three years ago, when I reported on the opening of Amoako Boafo’s residency dot.ateliers.

Accra Cultural Week includes studio visits, exhibition tours, talks, visits to cultural institutions, and social events. Artist-led spaces and an eclectic nightlife scene underscore how artistic production is shaped just as much by formal institutions as by the social and material conditions of the city’s close-knit communities.

Sources indicate that the week began with a performance at the studio of Serge Attukwei Clottey, the multidisciplinary artist who presented the gallery’s inaugural exhibition in 2016. Elsewhere, a tour of Boafo’s studio offered glimpses of work in progress. Just across the street, lunch at Backyard Community Club—a feast of fish stew, spicy jollof rice, and fried sweet plantains with chilled palm wine and sobolo, a local drink made of dried hibiscus, from Palm Moments—offered respite from the midday heat.

“The biggest thing that stands out to me is the sense of community and generosity here—not just from the gallery, but also the willingness of other artists and institutions to participate,” Nigerian artist Modupeola Fadugba says of Ghana’s art scene. “There is a leadership of community, which has led to more people following that leadership and being communal.” The story of Gallery 1957 is also the story of artists who have built their own institutions. Stops during Cultural Week included Kwesi Botchway’s WorldFaze Art Practice residency; El Anatsui’s studio, which employs dozens of people; and Rita Mawuena Benissan’s Si Hene Foundation.

According to recent reports, installation view: “Alvaro Barrington: “Western Beef ft. Western Union,” Limbo Museum, Accra.

In a recent development, the week continued with a stop at the Nubuke Foundation, now in its 20th year, and a visit to Alvaro Barrington’s exhibition “Western Beef ft. Western Union” at Limbo Museum, housed in an unfinished building on the University of Ghana campus. “The work we’re doing allows us to be radical, experimental, and to have the autonomy to define ourselves,” indicates the museum’s founder, Dominique Petit-Frère. “As an institution, we can offer artists opportunities to think beyond their practice.” Barrington, in turn, calls the show an “opportunity to present an artwork in Accra at a time when not only Ghana but the globe needs to reimagine how we grow.”.

Released in 2021, the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize—named after the Asante queen mother who led a resistance against British forces—provides support to African female artists. For the first time, it extends beyond Ghana to Senegalese women artists, offering a three-month residency exchange between Accra and Senegal, highlighting the gallery’s evolving ambitions.

“Where the Earth Remembers,” Gallery 1957’s 10th-anniversary exhibition, brings together a group of artists that “reflects the breadth and evolving scope” of the gallery’s program, featuring the work of Godfried Donkor, Serge Attukwei Clottey, Tunji Adeniyi-Jones, Rita Mawuena Benissan, Amoako Boafo, and Ibrahim Mahama, who has his own cultural centers, Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art (SCCA) and Red Clay Studio, both in Tamale, in Ghana’s Northern Region.

It has been revealed that at Red Clay, Ground Conditions: Tamale—a gathering presented by Limbo Museum and Studio Marant and supported by the Loewe Foundation—featured a conversation between Mahama and the Nigerian designer Nifemi Marcus-Bello. “There is something incredibly inspiring about witnessing his vision extend beyond his individual practice, into the creation of spaces that encourage dialogue, experimentation, and collective thinking,” Marcus-Bello says of Mahama.

Sources indicate that as the week ended, I reflected on the collaborations the gallery has forged, moving beyond mere visibility and toward engagement with the ideas and people that sustain the city’s cultural life. For Gallery 1957, the anniversary isn’t just a milestone—it’s also a testament to the artists and institutions that have taken root in its wake.

But these pull-ons were, in fact, from menswear favorite Merrell, built for some truly cold and ugly weather. The outer suede is water-resistant, the lining is insulated, and the rubber outsoles boast some serious traction. Plus, the very gorp-y utility cord at the heel lets you cinch them extra tight. Like the advanced-level dresser he is, Chalamet tucked his baggy black pants into the boots, making sure his footwear got a chance to really shine.

Once again, Chalamet has turned practical winter clothes into an A-list look. While a pink puffer might not be every guy’s idea of cold-weather dressing, there’s something to be stated for a winter coat with a little personality. Was celebrity row’s resident heartthrob a few weeks early with this ensemble? Sure, but when that first serious snowfall hits, he’ll be extra ready.

Fashion Wants You to Feel Something: ASMR Clothes That Chime, Rustle, and Ring

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (627 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that at Yuima Nakazato’s spring/summer 2026 haute couture show in January, the clothing was the soundtrack.
  • In a recent development, consider it a manifestation of the gentle brain massage we’re all craving amidst the chaos, even if just for a moment.
  • Industry observers note that “I chose not to add music to this show,” Nakazato wrote in his show notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that at Yuima Nakazato’s spring/summer 2026 haute couture show in January, the clothing was the soundtrack. Models paraded down the runway in slow motion while the chimes of hulking hand-sculpted ceramic beads rang out throughout the old church venue. The ASMR effect has slowly but surely started to make its way down the runways. In 2024, Paloma Wool had models showcase their clothing against microphones for the ultimate ASMR experience. Fast forward, and Simone Rocha has presented shoes topped with bells (an allusion to the classic English nursery rhyme); Celine’s embellished supersized paillette dresses gently rustled down the catwalk (begging to be touched) and Jean Paul Gaultier’s latest collections are covered in bells that softly jingle as they’re worn. Earlier this year, Maison Margiela showcased a shattered porcelain dress that emitted the sound of broken glass as the model wore it down the runway.

In a recent development, consider it a manifestation of the gentle brain massage we’re all craving amidst the chaos, even if just for a moment. Soothing sounds and clothing you can hear take a stab at promoting relaxation. At Nakazato’s show, the silence and the clinking of the clothing were a jolt. You could hear camera shutters and others’ breathing in between the footsteps of the models and the swaying of the heavy gowns: something typically impossible at most fashion shows.

Industry observers note that “I chose not to add music to this show,” Nakazato wrote in his show notes. “Today, we live surrounded by electronic sounds streaming through headphones and by the glow of screens, constantly absorbing information. That is why, during the fifteen minutes of this fashion show, I invite you to direct your attention to the unstable, subtle sounds created by the garments before you, and to the breath of the bodies wearing them.”.

Even if it’s trending now, clothing has a long history with ASMR qualities. Fashion has perpetually engaged beyond the visual sense, leveraging sound, texture, and movement to create a holistic tactile experience. Take, for instance, the time Viktor & Rolf famously covered garments in sonorous bells for their fall/winter 2000 couture collection, turning the runway into a symphony of sound. Yet even long before modern couture, women wore small bells stitched onto their garments in medieval Europe to signify presence and status, while in the 1850s, the distinct rustling sound of a big, full, and colorful skirt was widely regarded as an audible signifier of fashionable wealth and social standing.

According to recent reports, likewise, Jean Paul Gaultier’s bell-covered dress from spring/summer 2027 was inspired by a JPG glove from the 1989 archive, completely covered in tassels and bells. “When we started adding bells on things, it made an amazing sound,” creative director Duran Lantink said immediately following the show. “So we started thinking about that woman, or that person who is quite loud—she’s there, and she’s present.”.

Recent findings suggest that fashion’s ASMR love affair isn’t merely limited to sound either. Just look at fashion’s bags of the moment: intricately woven or designed to look like antique tapestries or grandma’s couch. Or Monse’s kinetic fringe, Bottega Veneta’s gasp-worthy fiberglass jackets, and Valentino’s awe-inspiring mermaid tail gowns resplendent in pleats and wrapped up with a black bow.

Noir Kei Ninomiya’s exploding garden dresses were blooming with dynamic flowers (both real and synthetic) with out-of-this-world silhouettes so tactile you get the feeling you might ascend to a higher place just by touching one.

In a recent development, maybe the urge to put our phones down and experience the real world (and all of its sounds, smells, and feels) is the most compelling thing about what’s coming down the runway right now. It’s fashion that wants to make you feel alive.

The Don of Denim has been the default brand for quality jeans—as well as every other wardrobe staple—for a century and a half, and it’s consistently been a go-to for bang-for-your-buck goods. Sources indicate that from brushed flannel shirts fit for a lumberjack to heirloom-level outerwear to, of course, legendary five-pocket blue jeans, Levi’s is doling out a grip of Black Friday deals with sitewide discounts up to 50% off. The best part? “Free shipping?” Good guess, but no. Free shipping is lumped in with some of the best Black Friday menswear deals going, but the actual “best part” is that you don’t even have to wait until Friday to snag the deals. The Levi’s Black Friday Sale starts today. Jumping the gun like that would end up poorly if this were a good ol’ fashioned illegal street race. In this case, it gets you kitted out in fresh gear.

You know them, love them, and need them: these are the originators, the one blue jean from which every other jean descends.

For the full denimhead experience, check out the 501 shrink-to-fit jeans and consider this the fade-it-yourself project of the winter.

According to recent reports, levi's got its start in honest-to-goodness workwear. And while the brand has expanded far beyond that, it's still essential to the DNA.

Selvedge jeans for a lot less than what you'd pay for a high-end pair from Japan.

A pair of hefty canvas work pants is also a must-have and, like we said, Levi's knows a thing or two about heavy-duty workwear.

Surprise, surprise—Levi's also perfected the bootcut jean.

Recent findings suggest that selvedge denim cut into a throwback Type I trucker silhouette for only how many bucks? Sign us up.

Is it a coincidence that the Levi's western shirt is also a certified classic? No.

If there's a case to be made to get yourself a simple, sturdy work jacket, it's this: it's gonna make you look handsome and this one is on sale.

Corduroy and cozy fleece sherpa make a hot couple, don't you think?

In a recent development, I might say that the Type II is the best iteration of the trucker jacket. Even better if you can get it in jet black for a steal.

In the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, the day after Thanksgiving, though many retailers roll out deals throughout November. Expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

It has been revealed that cyber Monday always falls on the Monday after Thanksgiving, which means this year it will be on November 30. Most Cyber Monday sales will extend through the end of the week, but that’s not a given.

What are the best things to buy at Levi’s?

Recent findings suggest that the brand is responsible for the blue jean as we know it, so it’s safe to say all things denim. Over the years, the 501 fit became catnip for a particular type of brooding all-American archetype—Brando in The Wild One, Dean in Rebel Without a Cause, Springsteen on the cover of Born in the U.S.A—and it’s still highly relevant today and also our pick for the best jeans.

#88961. Industry News: 31 Thanksgiving Dinner Alternatives to Turkey

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: 31 Thanksgiving Dinner Alternatives to Turkey

📅 18 Nov 2014 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that honestly, anything can make for an alternative Thanksgiving dinner.
  • It has been revealed that A classic Thanksgiving menu is all well and good, but one of our colleagues swears by serving nachos on the fourth Thursday of every November.
  • Or go completely rogue with lobster pasta or a big pot of chili.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that honestly, anything can make for an alternative Thanksgiving dinner. It’s your house, your rules. Our only suggestion: Make it festive, fun, and at least a little decadent.

It has been revealed that A classic Thanksgiving menu is all well and good, but one of our colleagues swears by serving nachos on the fourth Thursday of every November. If a big bloomin’ bird just isn’t ca-caw-caw-calling your name this year, serve a whole roast fish, pork tenderloin with sour-sweet cherry sauce, or a flaky carrot Wellington instead.

Or go completely rogue with lobster pasta or a big pot of chili. You can do that. Below, find vegetarian centerpieces, celebratory roasts, chicken dinners, and seafood mains for a Thanksgiving that looks a little different. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie can stay.

According to recent reports, can carrots really count as a main course? They can when they’re roasted, glazed, and tucked into puff pastry with goat cheese, Gruyère, and walnuts. This Wellington feeds 8 to 10.

Industry observers note that red wine, browned mushrooms, pearl onions, and carrots give this meatless braise plenty of heft. Ladle it over mashed potatoes for a vegetarian anchor to your Thanksgiving menu.

Industry observers note that ruffled savoy cabbage, melty cheese, and a buttery cream cheese crust make this free-form tart worthy of the holiday table. Cut generous wedges for dinner and stick with savoy: Ordinary green cabbage won’t work here.

It has been revealed that A make-ahead casserole, like this pumpkin-infused strata scented with nutmeg and herbs and balanced by sharp cheddar, is just what your holiday schedule needs. Assemble it the night before; bake it on Thanksgiving.

Turkey isn’t the only holiday cooking project worth clearing the counter for. Delicate homemade crepes are rolled around ricotta, mozzarella, and Parmesan, then baked in marinara. Make the batter and filling a day ahead to split up the work.

Industry observers note that kale, pinto beans, and charred poblanos make these cheesy enchiladas a satisfying holiday main for four to six. Get a head start by making the charred salsa verde up to three days ahead.

This autumnal risotto works as a standalone dinner or alongside your favorite Thanksgiving sides. Set the table with shallow bowls and pick a fall salad full of color and crunch to balance the buttery rice.

Sources indicate that british beef Wellington meets Cantonese barbecue-style pork in Peter Som’s pastry-wrapped centerpiece. A shiitake mushroom filling and gravy made from the marinade complete the picture; assemble the Wellington a day ahead.

These impossibly tender short ribs are begging to be served with mashed potatoes and buttery milk buns with garlic butter. Give them what they want—and give yourself a head start by braising the ribs the day before Thanksgiving.

Brisket more your speed? Try our Brisket Bourguignon →.

Turkey skin has competition. Tender pork belly, crisp crackling, and a hard cider pan sauce make a persuasive case for skipping the bird. Pass the chile vinegar to cut through the richness; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

According to recent reports, ayesha Curry’s spice-crusted prime rib takes its cues from her mother’s braised oxtails, with habanero crema on the side. Prefer a simpler garlic-and-rosemary approach? Try this Low-and-Slow Rib Roast.

For a roast-and-sides Thanksgiving without the turkey, garlic-and-rosemary-rubbed beef tenderloin makes an excellent centerpiece. Rosemary butter dresses the sliced roast, while tangy horseradish yogurt gives everyone something to swipe their next bite through.

Toasted rice, fried onions, and garlic form a dark, peppery crust on this slow-braised pork shoulder. Set out the big platter and pass the coconut-vinegar pan sauce; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Maybe save the brown sugar-glazed ham for Christmas? This whole leg of lamb makes for a centerpiece that’s just as showstopping. And, like ham and turkey, leftover lamb can be deliciously repurposed in sandwiches.

A platter of sliced pork tenderloin with glossy cherries and browned shallots has plenty of holiday presence without a long roast. Honey and red wine vinegar give the sauce its sweet-sour bite, and frozen cherries are welcome here.

If you’re going to make tamales, it’s a good idea to make a lot of them. Better yet, turn the process into a party, with everyone spreading masa and folding corn husks around the red chile pork filling.

In a recent development, this pasta packs a whole spectrum of holiday flavors into each bite, with crumbles of Italian sausage, shreds of brussels sprouts, and toasted pecans. Streamlining dinner into one dish leaves you more time for Thanksgiving pies.

For some people, spending all Thanksgiving in the kitchen sounds like a good time. For everyone else, there’s this beef-and-bean chili. A can of pumpkin purée thickens the broth, keeping things seasonal without calling for a single roasting pan.

Give homemade fried chicken an even more festive angle with sage and thyme in the dredge and cranberry-mustard sauce for dipping. Start the buttermilk marinade the day before.

Industry observers note that this whole roast duck comes with a built-in Thanksgiving side: The duck fat drippings go into basmati rice that cooks while the bird rests. Strategy for an overnight dry brine before the glossy pomegranate-honey glaze gets its moment.

It has been revealed that cooking for a smaller crowd? This skillet delivers the stuffing and the bird—chicken thighs, in this case—in one tidy package. Rendered chicken fat enriches the boxed stuffing mix, with dried cranberries and lemon zest brightening things up.

It has been revealed that two diminutive birds make a festive roast for four. A fiery guajillo chile, ginger, and vinegar marinade flavors both the hens and the potatoes beneath them, so the platter arrives with its own very good side.

You just need to make green beans, because this Thanksgiving main is already a two-in-one: Thinly sliced potatoes cook beneath a whole chicken, catching its drippings and crisping around the edges in the same cast-iron skillet.

Sources indicate that if your Thanksgiving table could use a little red sauce (and spice), skip the whole bird in favor of this take on chicken parm. Gochujang and gochugaru bring the heat; melted mozzarella keeps things gloriously gooey.

José Andrés turns chicken wings and a colorful assortment of vegetables into a grand centerpiece, with saffron and smoked paprika flavoring the rice. You’ll need a 15" paella pan or comparably sized two-handled cast-iron or cast-aluminum pan.

Sources indicate that there’s nothing like pasta to stretch a spendy ingredient (hello, lobster). Serve with a major crunchy salad with Italian dressing and garlic confit toast that diners can pass around for Thanksgiving party vibes.

According to recent reports, presenting a whole fish at the holiday table is wildly celebratory, even when you’re cooking for just two or three. Bring out lettuce wraps, kimchi, rice, and ssamjang so everyone can build each bite a little differently.

A large roasted salmon fillet looks right at home on a holiday platter, especially under a crunchy, garlicky nut salsa. Make the salsa up to four days ahead, then roast the fish when it’s time for dinner.

The stuffing doesn’t have to be a side. Here, crushed boxed stuffing mix joins Parmesan, lemon zest, and parsley in a crisp crust for mustard-coated white fish. Dinner lands on the table in 25 minutes.

This dark, glossy coconut caramel—savory with fish sauce and garlic, sharp with pickled jalapeño brine—turns pan-seared salmon into a holiday-worthy main. Serve with rice to catch every last bit of sauce.

Sources indicate that like many of the best Thanksgiving dishes, this one starts with a good stock. Carla Hall builds a fennel potlikker with celery, onions, and Pernod before layering those flavors into a hearty bowl of shrimp and grits.

#88960. Setting Up Shop in Istanbul

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3399 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

Setting Up Shop in Istanbul

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in Istanbul, hosts encourage guests to stay as long as they like — even in luxury department stores.
  • In a recent development, the store is located in Galataport, a cultural and shopping district adjacent to the Bosphorus, the strait separating Türkiye’s European and Asian sides.
  • In a recent development, beyond luxury retail, Istanbul and Türkiye are widely renowned for their role in the textile and leather industries, home to a large portion of the major clothing manufacturers used by Western brands, including Isko Denim, Kipaş and Bilsar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in Istanbul, hosts encourage guests to stay as long as they like — even in luxury department stores. “We want our client to spend time here, to sit here, to play backgammon, to chat, to have a drink,” states Sebla Refiğ Devidas, chief merchandising officer at Communité, a new concept-department store hybrid, first opened in April of this year, with two outposts on the European side of the city. “We wanted to give a homey, warm feeling,” she adds, guiding me through the retailer’s second location, opened in May. Unlike many of Istanbul’s retail spaces, the store features windows throughout, letting natural sunlight fill the curving, geometric shop-in-shops, clean furnishings, and marble plinths. We pass rails of brands including Martine Rose, Simone Rocha and Auralee, as well as a warmly lit Mayfair-style restaurant, a glass-paneled red-light therapy salon and box vitrines of jewellery by Turkish jewellery designer Sevan Bıçakçı.

In a recent development, the store is located in Galataport, a cultural and shopping district adjacent to the Bosphorus, the strait separating Türkiye’s European and Asian sides. Galataport is also home to a number of luxury players. Beymen — Türkiye’s answer to Bergdorf Goodman — has an outpost. There’s also a Vakkorama, the luxury retailer Vakko’s accessible, contemporary store. And Turkish design-focused luxury chain Gizia Gate. Together, these four names (Communité, Beymen, Vakko and Gizia Gate) define the Turkish fashion landscape, taking the lion’s share of a relatively small fashion retail market.

In a recent development, beyond luxury retail, Istanbul and Türkiye are widely renowned for their role in the textile and leather industries, home to a large portion of the major clothing manufacturers used by Western brands, including Isko Denim, Kipaş and Bilsar. Value-seeking shoppers also enjoy the region’s stores specializing in factory seconds — lightly defective branded apparel sold at a discount — and counterfeit luxury goods available in the historic Grand Bazaar, where sellers are naturally averse to photography.

Sebla Refiğ Devidas (left) works as the chief merchandizing officer at Communité.

Istanbul has a population of more than 15 million people, while Türkiye has over 86 million. According to data from Euromonitor, Türkiye’s market for luxury goods delivered steady growth in 2025, recovering from continued macroeconomic pressures. High-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) remained a core driver for growth, while inflation — exacerbated by the Middle East crisis — dragged on discretionary spending for middle-income groups. The report also cited Gucci, Hermès, Prada and Louis Vuitton as some of the leading international brands in the personal luxury goods category. In 2026, Euromonitor forecasts luxury sales to reach almost $28 billion in 2026, over double the revenue in 2021.

“Istanbul sits at the heart of this opportunity, supported by growing domestic wealth alongside its strength as an international shopping, hospitality and cultural destination,” claims Fflur Roberts, Euromonitor International’s head of luxury. Tourism is becoming particularly key, she adds, noting that international visitors now account for 29% of personal luxury goods spending in Türkiye, up from 20% in 2019. “Wealthy Russian travelers have contributed to this shift, as geopolitical developments redirect travel and luxury spending toward markets including Türkiye and the UAE.”.

Outside Communité’s fresh location in Galataport.

Presently, Roberts reports, online channels account for 21% of personal luxury sales in Türkiye — which is more than double the share in 2015. “Yet physical retail remains key, giving Istanbul an opportunity to combine global luxury brands with Turkish fashion, craftsmanship, hospitality, gastronomy and culture as consumers increasingly blend shopping with travel and experiences,” Roberts affirms.

Within this relatively small retail pond, luxury retail competition is fierce.

Sources indicate that and competition is heating up. Communité will open two more stores on the European side and one on the Asian side in 2027, complementing a strong online presence. The retailer is owned by Boyner, which originally founded Beymen in 1970. Beymen has now changed ownership: since 2015, the Qatari fund Mayhoola has been investing in the retailer, eventually taking control in 2019.

Inside Communité, clients can inquire about buying the furniture.

Devidas was a merchandising lead at Beymen, but in August 2024, following a five-year non-compete clause, she and many of her former colleagues from Boyner jumped ship to the newly founded Communité. “We didn't want to repeat what we had done,” she notes. “But we wanted to create something newly introduced from scratch.” During the research stage, the team traveled the globe, informing their objectives for clienteling, product assortments and dwell time. Hospitality will prove integral to its value proposition, she says.

Insiders respect it, too. Cemre Bosnalı Zeydanlı, Vogue Türkiye’s strategy editor, pinpoints the retailer as exemplary of Türkiye’s retail development: “With its locations at İstinye Park and Galataport, the concept goes beyond traditional multi-brand retail by bringing together fashion, beauty, design, culture and lifestyle.”.

Recent findings suggest that on my visit to Communité, Devidas tells me that much of the furniture in the store is available to buy. There are Turkish brands — Lug Von Siga, for example — alongside mega international brands, including Japanese streetwear giant A Bathing Ape (Bape), which Devidas says is a Communité exclusive in Türkiye.

Industry observers note that taking a more traditionally luxe approach, Beymen Group is ramping up its retail presence across the country. The retail giant owns 290 stores in various formats across Türkiye and Egypt (a small operation): 25 multi-brand, 60 franchise stores with leading designer brands, and three of its own brands. The expansion is in progress.

During my stay in the city, Beymen underscores its luxury ambitions with a ritzy event program, built around a new exhibition, Timeless Treasures — an homage to traditional Anatolian envelope bags through the lens of contemporary Western and local designers — at its flagship location in the wealthy shopping and hospitality district of Tersane. The exhibition coincides with the OMA-designed store’s first anniversary and intends to bridge a gap between the Turkish and global fashion landscape.

Industry observers note that toasting the occasion, Beymen invited industry authorities and fashion designers Giuseppe Zanotti, Giuseppe Santoni and Antonin Tron to a black-tie gala. During the evening, brand execs rubbed shoulders with Beymen group’s senior leadership team as group CEO Elif Çapçı outlined her vision for Beymen and the future of Türkiye’s fashion landscape. Diana Ross performed afterwards.

High-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) typically lead consumer spending for Beymen, and the organization — thanks to Mayhoola’s investment — is courting this, enhancing its store experiences and private-shopping service. Beymen has no plans to expand globally and will focus almost entirely on Türkiye.

Beymen’s Tersane location was designed with the Office for Metropolitan Architecture (OMA).

The reason for Beymen’s focus on the home market? It needs to feel rooted in the location. “The department store is more like a house that you bring people to,” states Rachid Mohamed Rachid, Mayhoola CEO and chairman for Valentino and Balmain. “People have to be comfortable with the culture, with the DNA, with the approach.” This fiscal year, the group is close to making €1.5 billion, growing at 15% in the first nine months.

Industry observers note that while Communité’s footprint doesn’t quite compete with Beymen, Vakko’s — opened first as a small hat shop in 1934 — does. As of March 31, the manufacturer has 150 stores and remains a household name in Türkiye. The company offers a variety of categories, own-brand goods and store formats including Vakkorama, Vakko Couture (a fashion-forward boutique) and the original Vakko luxury stores.

Tarik, 28, a sales adviser in Vakkorama.

Sources indicate that tarik, 28, works in Vakkorama’s Galataport location. He explains that customers engage with the retailer for its fashion-forward choice of brands evidenced in the V2K Designers range — Marni, Thom Browne, JW Anderson, for example — as well as unique pieces from brands, such as Adidas, that can’t be found elsewhere in the country.

“I think multi-brand stores such as V2K Designers play an important role in Istanbul’s fashion ecosystem,” notes Zeydanlı. ”Being able to explore collections from different designers in one place brings a more curated perspective to shopping.”.

Vakko — which own sub-brands V2K, Vakkorama, and Vakko Couture — is one of the significant four in the Turkish retail market.

For local Turkish designers, landing one of the big four wholesalers can be hard, especially if you’re an emerging voice. When Gul Agis, the designer behind established Turkish brand Lug Von Siga, started out 17 years ago after studying in Italy, she actually focused on reaching stores across mainland Europe, taking part in fashion weeks and trade demonstrates in Berlin, Paris and Milan. “It was quite challenging for me because where Milan was quite professional in prêt-à-porter, it was almost the beginning here [in Istanbul],” she remembers. “Most of the fashion houses or designers used to do more haute couture or made-to-measure pieces.”.

Sources indicate that at the time, she says that the major Turkish retailers tended to focus on foreign brands. Fast forward to now, and a lot has changed. Lug Von Siga has since been stocked by Beymen and Gizia Gate, although those partnerships have now ended. Today, she works with Vakko and Communité, plus a myriad of European stockists including Harvey Nichols, Farfetch and Harrods.

Vakkorama’s Galataport location faces a waterway used by cruise ships.

Industry observers note that istanbul’s retail landscape is substantial on malls, comprising key new-build districts such as Tersane, Galataport and Zorlu Center. Shoppers take their time while purchasing, sipping coffee or Turkish tea, and store advisors provide discretion and advice where necessary for private clients. The shopping experience is slower and more relaxed, compared to fashion hubs like London and New York.

Consumers in Istanbul rely on malls such as Zorlu Center on the European side.

Beyond these purpose-built complexes, Istanbul is also home to an even more easygoing, hilly, open shopping district, Nişantaşı, on the European side of the city. Here, Prada, Chanel, Beymen, Vakko, and other major players have stores, as well as a substantial number of concept stores. Turkish fashion photographer Fırat Koçak, who joins me on the journey, describes Nişantaşı as a trendier district, with many editors, stylists and photographers living here. National treasure designer Ozgur Masur’s showroom is here, as well as Agis’s.

Nişantaşı’s Shopi Go is a perennial hangout for cool kids. Opened in 2012 in a former Chinese food joint, complete with exposed-brick walls, the cozy two-story store is arranged with coffee-table books, knick-knacks, and niche fashion apparel. Y-3’s cleat football sneakers, Wales Bonner x Umbro designs, and pieces from underground Turkish label Doomster fill the space. It’s charmingly dingy, and the product assortment is esoteric, clearly aimed at a more niche Turkish consumer.

Shopi Go is a Chinese-food-spot-turned concept store.

Shopi Go is aimed at the more directional Turkish consumer, offering Wales Bonner x Umbro through to local brand Doomster.

Industry observers note that A few blocks away, two smiling buyers — Emir Akdogan and Dylon Kader — sit outside the streetwear store Wunder’s largest location. They’ve agreed to show me around. Inside, the architecture is restrained, cold and contemporary — a far cry from the more luxe DTC stores peppered elsewhere in the area. Wunder’s first store opened in 2015 in Kadikoy, a district on the Asian side, and rapidly capitalized on the sneaker boom. In 2021, Wunder opened the Nişantaşı store. Today, it continues to push anticipated sneakers from Nike (including Jordan) and Salomon, as well as streetwear from brands including Stüssy, Carhartt and Stockholm Surfboard Club.

It has been revealed that “I assume we are the only super-contemporary store, rather than a department store [in Istanbul], which makes us slightly different,” states Akdogan. “Still, sneakers are a huge part of the business,” says Kader. “We were one of the stores that had camps — first come, first served. People put tents in the streets. It was so newly introduced to the Turkish community, and the Turkish market, so it was not done before.”.

In Istanbul, stray cats are treated with reverence and free neutering. They’re not typically allowed in stores, though.

In a recent development, akdogan and Kader describe the Turkish market as a little slower to catch on to hot European market trends. The pair tells me that they had to convince the Salomon global team to come to Türkiye. When Salomon agreed, two to three years ago, Wunder began selling the brand. “The first three or four seasons, it didn’t sell at all — even with discounts,” remembers Kader. “Then last season, something happened. People started to ask for Salomons, and we started to bump up our orders.”.

The buyers want to set trends and be global, but contend that does involve some business sacrifice as the national market catches up with global trends. That said, the most loyal consumer for Wunder is an educated shopper, the pair confirm.

Emir Akdogan and Dylon Kader are buyers at Wunder, one of the original streetwear stores in the city.

Recent findings suggest that “Türkiye is a dynamic market for fashion and luxury, but one shaped by its own economic and cultural nuances,” says Zeydanlı. “One of the most interesting aspects of the Turkish market, in my opinion, is the consumer’s interest in both global fashion houses and local designers.” Zeydanlı encourages brands looking to enter the Turkish market to understand local consumer expectations, developing the right pricing strategy to handle growing price sensitivity among consumers.

Beymen’s chief merchandising officer, Ahmet Öcal, explains that the tech giant’s buying strategy is rooted in a deep understanding of their clients’ lifestyles. “We serve a diverse and increasingly sophisticated customer base through Beymen’s extensive brand curation and personalized service approach, ranging from established luxury clients who value heritage, craftsmanship and timeless elegance, to younger, fashion-forward consumers who are looking for newness, individuality and self-expression,” he explains, noting that the core consumer base is local, while 15% are international tourists.

In a recent development, “Occasion wear, elevated casualwear, luxury handbags, jewelry, cosmetics, and beauty are particularly relevant categories for our market,” indicates Öcal. “Resort wear is another vital area, reflecting the lifestyle of our customers and their connection to destinations like Bodrum.”.

“When it comes to clienteling, I believe the emphasis should be on genuinely understanding the customer: their personal style, preferences and shopping habits,” notes Zeydanlı. “Curated product selections, early access to upcoming collections, private shopping appointments, and invitations to exclusive brand experiences all play an notable role.” This chimes with the kind of customer engagement strategies Beymen employs, maintaining close and enduring relations with top spenders, many of whom have shopped there for years.

Recent findings suggest that across the board, luxury players cite millennials as a strong consumer in the Turkish retail landscape, particularly those within the 30 to 40 bracket. Beymen’s target consumer is roughly 35-plus. That said, players should ensure they speak to younger generations. For Zeydanlı, Gen Z might not have the strongest purchasing power yet, but they remain a key consumer group shaping the future of luxury. “Gen X, meanwhile, remains an important segment, particularly among high-net-worth consumers, thanks to more established luxury shopping habits and stronger brand loyalty,” she says.

The city of Istanbul is relatively young in the global luxury retail market, despite its strong manufacturing heritage. “However, on the design side, we are lacking certain components that would make our designers global names and successful on a global scale,” notes Mayhoola’s Rachid. “The visibility is not there.”.

Setting up shop here as a local independent designer remains risky, although it’s improving. Across the board, international household names rule the market.

Sources indicate that however, as the market grows, tastes could shift. While Beymen might choose to focus its efforts on the local demand, the Istanbul region still has plenty of white space. “We see an notable distinction between generations,” says Öcal. “While our more established customers tend to prioritize quality, exclusivity and long-term value, Gen Z and younger millennials are more experimental, trend-conscious and open to discovering emerging designers and brands.”.

In a recent development, the importance of physical retail in Türkiye is another advantage. Euromonitor’s findings revealed that brick-and-mortar stores dominated personal luxury goods distribution in the nation last year.

Beymen’s Tersane flagship location opened last year.

In a recent development, “The importance high-net-worth consumers place on personalized service and exclusive shopping experiences makes physical stores indispensable for luxury brands,” argues Zeydanlı. “I believe independent designers and local brands are becoming increasingly visible. Consumers are looking beyond global fashion houses and are also interested in discovering brands with a distinctive design identity, more limited production and a unique creative perspective.”.

Communité is an experiment in the market. Prospective competitors will be watching closely to see if it lands or if it’s just too soon.

Industry observers note that matt, 45, a firm owner based in Istanbul, is trying on a Beymen Club (the group’s own brand) knit in Beymen’s Galataport location. He opts for brands that aren’t “too vulgar”, preferring what he calls “silent luxury”. “I don’t like clothing with huge brand [logos] on them,” he notes. “This is one of the places you can find the stuff that [I’m] looking for.” Annually, his typical clothing spend sits at no more than around $5,000 per year. “I don’t shop very often to be honest with you,” he says. For Matt, the country’s luxury sector isn’t especially different from other countries, although he does note a preference among consumers for more visibly branded clothing.

It has been revealed that originally from Germany, Ayliz, 22, owns her own brand. Her store is around the corner. She’s posing for a photo in Nişantaşı when I stop her to ask what she makes of the Turkish fashion landscape. “I think Türkiye follows world trends. So, people my age, we wear things that are viral now on social media,” she claims. As a shopper, she’s drawn to high luxury, citing Loro Piana and Chanel, and she prefers physical retail. “100% in-person. I have to feel the texture, and see how it looks on me.” She sees Türkiye as a place where you can shop “everything you want”, offering far more stores than her home country.

Miray, 43, an executive vice president in marketing and sales, is taking a meeting in Zorlu Center mall. She used to shop here, but nowadays less so, as she right now resides on the Anatolian side of the city. For her, Türkiye is unique for its customer experience. “Beymen provides a very unique experience,” she claims. The store is special because of its brand offering and ease, and she has shopped with the retailer for more than 10 years. She does admit, however, that sometimes she buys brands in Europe (London or France), where they can be cheaper. “I love Burberry, but I’m not a fan of only one brand,” she says. “If I see something good, I buy it. Price and quality are key, and experience also — very crucial.”.

Burak, 49, a cost controller in the restaurant sector, prefers shopping online. He’s in the Zorlu Center when I bump into him. He likes brands such as Levi’s and Carhartt for apparel, while for footwear, he opts for Nike and Autry. He’s also into Japanese brands, which he noticed on a visit to Communité. What does he think is unique about Türkiye’s fashion landscape? “It’s mostly haute couture, dresses — I don’t see any [local] designers. They [the retailers] buy outsider [brands], but I don’t like them.”.

Başak, 48, at the moment unemployed, is visiting Zorlu Center mall. She lives on the Asian side, so would typically shop in the Emaar Square Mall. She tells me she isn’t committed to any specific brands, although I note her Michael Kors bag. “When I have the time, I like to shop in person,” she indicates, although she enjoys both online and physical retail. Her approach to shopping? Meet friends, then shop.

It has been revealed that born and raised in Istanbul, 24-year-old graduate Umut tells me his name means “hope” in English. He’s just dropped into Shopi Go in Nişantaşı and is now standing outside. What brands does he like? “For T-shirts, I like Prada, but for sunglasses, I like Off-White — the Virgil [Abloh] versions,” he indicates. These days, he typically opts for Adidas footwear. “I don’t like the fresh Nike designs.” As for his thoughts on Nişantaşı: “It’s mostly luxury. You feel like it’s better quality here.”.

Latest Update: Nigella Lawson’s Best Baking Advice Of All Time

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson.
  • From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.
  • Cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson. If she told me to put sardines in a birthday cake, I’d believe her. That’s just the kind of culinary authority you earn after nearly three decades of making us hungry through the TV screen. The cookbook author and television personality is now dishing out advice on The Great British Baking Show—she made her debut as a GBBS judge in September—but it’s just a small window into her extensive wisdom.

From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.

Cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does. “I think every recipe has to be as precise as possible,” Lawson told Vogue in 2018. “Baking, you have to be really precise. If you’re cooking and it suggests 2 to 3 carrots, it doesn’t really matter because they can be different sizes. It’s not going to alter the taste.”.

So, you’ve never really baked before. It’s okay to start small! A three-tier chantilly cake your first day in the kitchen probably isn’t your best bet. “It’s key to go for a simple recipe. Read through the recipe to make sure you understand everything that’s being told to you at the time,” she said. “Look for a recipe that gives you an indication of what to do at each stage. This is what I always say to people: remind yourself you’re not running a restaurant.”.

If you’ve been making your chocolate cake with milk, here’s your sign to stop. Lawson suggests swapping the dairy for hot or boiling water instead to “bloom” the cocoa, dissolve the sugar, and loosen the batter. The result? A crazy moist crumb!

Instead of using plain water when baking bread, Lawson suggests swapping it out for leftover pasta or potato water. “It will help the bread’s texture and rise,” she wrote on X in 2020. “Taste it before adding, though. If very salty, dilute it with fresh water and, obviously, leave any salt in the recipe out.”.

It might sound weird, but Lawson swears by cream of tartar for fluffier, softer scones. “These are the best [ones] I’ve ever eaten, which is quite how it should be since they emanate from one of those old-fashioned cooks who starts a batch the minute the doorbell rings at teatime,” she wrote on her website in 2017. “Yes, I know they look as if they’ve got cellulite—it’s the cream of tartar, which is also why, despite their apparent solidity, they have that dreamy lightness.”.

Sources indicate that lawson’s genius baking hack? DIY self-rising flour. “Nigella tends not to use self-raising flour in her more recent books as she doesn’t bother to keep both plain (all-purpose) and self-raising flour,” her site reads. “Partly because keeping just one type of flour saves on storage space, and partly because if you don’t use self-raising flour regularly, then it will lose its raising power over time.”.

Sources indicate that instead, simply add 2 teaspoons of baking powder for each cup of plain flour. Sift the flour and baking powder together into a bowl before using (and make sure the baking powder is fully integrated), and you’re golden!

Sources indicate that we’re all a little extra busy around the holidays, so if you’re planning a dinner party or holiday get-together, it’s okay to make shortcuts. Even Lawson claims not everything has to be baked from scratch.

“I have a bit of a weakness for this sort of cake, which is essentially an assembly-job number, a construction of alternate layers of a rich, boozy cream and some store-bought sponge or other,” she told the BBC in 2023 about one of her favorite holiday desserts. “Here the layers comprise a confection of cream and mascarpone, seasonally spiked with Advocaat, full of crystallized ginger, figs and nuts, and that essential component of Christmas: gingerbread.”.

Even Lawson admits: “just the words ‘uniformity of size and shape’ make [her] quake.” Hello, crazy foreshadowing for her future on GBBS.

“I am not in the slightest bit insecure about what I can bake, and I’m so very happy doing it, but shop-bought perfection is way beyond me,” she mentioned in a 2014 interview with The Guardian. “But I’m perfectly content with that, and with the ramshackle homemade-ness of my creations.” If that’s good enough for Nigella, it’s good enough for me!
